articles.title: South Africa v Australia: third men’s cricket Test, day three – live
articles.summary: Updates as the Proteas host the series decider at Newlands Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email 93rd over: Australia 338-4 (Inglis 90, Carey 54) Jansen wakes up Carey with a shorter ball. He gets the ball angling into the left-hander before ending the over with two more bouncers. Maiden. 92nd over: Australia 338-4 (Inglis 90, Carey 54) Wiaan Mulder takes the ball for South Africa. Have to think Kagiso Rabada is still feeling below full fitness as he stands in the field with his side desperate for an early breakthrough or two. Gerald Coetzee dives over the ball at mid-on and it races away to the boundary. It was an exquisite straight drive from Inglis and Coetzee got an unlucky bounce. But that is two little slices of misfortune that have already struck the Proteas today. Continue reading...
articles.content:
What is actually going on?! Bedingham wafts at a short ball with no control, no thought, no appreciation for the game situation or what his team needs, and sends a top edge straight to Lyon down at deep square. Utterly bizarre. South Africa are throwing this series away.

7th over: South Africa 31-1 (Ackerman 15, Bedingham 11) A lot of cricket in this Starc over. It begins with a lovely square drive for four from Bedingham. Then a firmer, more imperious cover drive screams off the bat but it’s well fielded. A bumper turns Bedingham into a T-rex as he lifts his hands awkwardly, lucky not to have the ball loop to a fielder. He closes the eventful set with a tuck off his pads for one down to fine leg. Starc runs off the park. He was little a little niggly, but he lopes up the stairs which suggests he’s OK.

6th over: South Africa 26-1 (Ackerman 15, Bedingham 6) They’re definitely targeting Ackerman with the short ball. There’s a catcher under the helmet in place. He swishes at a pull shot but can’t get a hold of it. Then he tucks a single off his hips. Bedingham drops into the off side for one before a thick inside edge from Ackerman’s prodding blade gets him one down to deep square. Bedingham slices a drive through cover for one. He wanted two but was rightly sent back by his partner.

5th over: South Africa 22-1 (Ackerman 13, Bedingham 4) Starc bangs in a bumper but it almost bounces on his own toes, that’s how short it was. It digs into the pitch and comfortabley clears a leaping Carey as it bobbles away for four bonus runs for the Proteas. Super quick, though. He’s touching the 150km/h mark. Ackerman does well off the last ball, riding the bounce to tuck a single through square leg.

“6-55 feels like another Aussie collapse but no mention at all? Interesting.”

4th over: South Africa 16-1 (Ackerman 12, Bedingham 3) The Australians placed such a high price on their wickets. The South Africans have not learned any lessons. After Markram gave away his wicket, Ackerman is wafting at a back of a length ball from Hazlewood that rises as it kisses the surface and moves across him. Ackerman scampers a single either side of a pair of ones for Bedingham. This pitch is only going to get harder to bat on, though it still looks decent now. South Africa have to bat for as long as they can to make a game of this.

3rd over: South Africa 13-1 (Ackerman 11, Bedingham 1) Starc has bagged early wickets throughout his career but surely none have come easier than that. Markram will be livid back in the shed as he’s put his team in trouble with that soft dismissal. Bedingham, off the mark with a single down to deep point from his first ball, has a proper job to do now.

What has Aiden Markram done?! I’ll tell you, but if you’re South African you won’t like it. A full ball, but not a half volley, from Starc is driven firmly but in the air and straight to Head at mid-off. Such a poor shot from such a quality player. That is the frustration with a batter who can look like a dream but haunt your nightmares if you’re willing him to produce on a more consistent basis. Starc with a gimme and the Aussies are rolling.

2nd over: South Africa 7-0 (Markram 1, Ackerman 6) Hazlewood is bang on the money from the off, as you’d expect. He beats Ackerman by going across the left hander from over the wicket and then finds the edge from his second ball. But it’s played with soft hands flies through a gap between third slip and gully for four. There is a leg slip and Hazlewood bangs it in short and pings Ackerman on the body. The follow up is a gem, beating the outside edge again, squaring him up. He’ll keep the strike again with a little flick down to fine leg.

1st over: South Africa 2-0 (Markram 1, Ackerman 1) Starc is finding early movement back into Markram. One is pushed fuller and there’s a big appeal for an lbw, but there was clear bat on it. A shorter one allows Markram to stand tall and steer it to a fielder who is already stationed at deep point (I know it’s the way of the modern world, but I don’t quite get that). Ackerman survives the two balls he has to face, dropping into the covers and running to get off the mark.

Thanks Martin. What a stint from you, and what a game this is! Australia’s to lose from here, of course, but anything can happen. The pitch is flat (for now) and is threatening to turn loads on days four and five.

It’s hard to walk away from closely watching such a gripping Test. But Daniel Gallan is ready and waiting to take the reins for the rest of day three as South Africa look to knock off their 100-run deficit then … who knows what will happen from there?!?

Thanks for following along, I’m heading to the sofa to watch the rest of the day’s play …

Australia have compiled a 100-run lead off the back of a second Test century for Josh Inglis (102) and important contributions from Alex Carey (80) and openers Matt Renshaw (74) and Travis Head (41). Cooper Connolly (29) showed promising signs in his second Test as he battled hard for every run while batting with the tail to keep the South African bowlers toiling away. Simon Harmer (4 for 104) was the standout bowler as he made the most of the pitch that looks set to give spinners plenty to work with. Marco Jansen (3 for 60) was below his best today but wrapped up the innings with a fine catch.

Advantage Australia! But surely we’ve learned to expect more twists in the tale to come with the halfway point of the Test series decider now just minutes away.

Connolly finally looks to open up with Australia’s No 11 at the crease but mistimes the straight drive and Jansen takes a sharp caught and bowled chance.

125th over: Australia 429-9 (Connolly 29, Hazlewood 4) Mulder finds a way through Lyon’s defences to get his reward for a good spell. Hazlewood steps the crease and immediately clobbers a sublime drive through cover for four. The Australia lead reaches 100 runs.

Mulder has been troubling Lyon with outswingers since lunch and finally he gets his man. Lyon reaches to prod at a delivery heading for the imaginary fifth stump but can only get an edge to Harmer at second slip who dives low to his right to grasp the chance.

124th over: Australia 425-8 (Connolly 29, Lyon 1) Ooft! Jansen gives Connolly a working over with a short-pitched barrage at varying pace and height. The young Australian keeps his gloves down for a slower bouncer that stays lower than the pitch suggested. But then fails to pick up another bouncer as he ducks and turns his head at the next delivery that fails to get up. The ball crashes into Connolly’s helmet and he needs some attention before eventually being allowed to play on. Maiden.

123rd over: Australia 425-8 (Connolly 29, Lyon 1) Mulder has two slips, a gully and the ball moving away from Lyon as the Australian tailender can’t help play along. Lyon prods and gets an edge flying towards Harmer in the cordon but the ball bounces just before it reaches the fielder. A fine over and a maiden.

122nd over: Australia 425-8 (Connolly 29, Lyon 1) Jansen picks up the pace with South Africa otherwise offering little threat since lunch. Connolly punishes a half-volley with a blazing drive through cover to the rope. That’s one way to keep the scoreboard ticking over while staying on strike. But this time Connolly is unable to find a single late in the over as Jansen ends it with a bouncer.

121st over: Australia 421-8 (Connolly 25, Lyon 1) Connolly works Mulder behind square for a single as Lyon is left with two balls to face. Clever batting from the relatively young Australian.

120th over: Australia 420-8 (Connolly 24, Lyon 1) Jansen keeps staking his claim to be the best cricketer in the family as he holds Australia to a leg-bye.

“Daniel Gallan’s otherwise entertaining take on Marco inexplicably failed to mention that the Jansen family lab bioengineered two cricketers, and at the same time. What stars the Jansen parents are!” Stephen Gelb says. “Duan has already played white ball cricket for SA and hopefully one day soon we’ll see the two of them playing a test together.”

To save you searching too far down the OBO, here is Daniel’s story again …

119th over: Australia 419-8 (Connolly 24, Lyon 1) Mulder takes the ball as South Africa begin with the same pair as in the first session. Connolly drives a half-volley for two through cover and picks up a single as Mulder comes around the wicket and drifts on to his pads. Lyon swings at a ball that darts down the leg side but Mulder is too good to find the bat or keeper’s gloves for four byes.

118th over: Australia 412-8 (Connolly 21, Lyon 1) Connolly picks up where he left off before lunch as he keeps Jansen out with South Africa left-arm quick working away back of a length. But Connolly can’t resist a shorter ball as he gets under a pull shot and is happy to see it drop safely in a vacant deep backward square. Once again Australia turn down a run as Connolly takes a single to keep the strike.

The players are heading back out on to the Newlands field after lunch. Interesting to note that four of the five Tests since that infamous day in 2018 have been won by the side chasing down their fourth innings target, even if the most recent match at the start of 2025 included South Africa forcing Pakistan to follow on.

Cooper Connolly is on strike as Australia try to build a commanding first innings lead. Marco Jansen has the ball in hand to begin his attempts to do the opposite. Let’s play …

If you were to bioengineer a cricketer in a laboratory, which attributes would you give them? You would make them tall, with long limbs and a whiplash action to extract steep bounce. Add speed, movement both ways and a left arm to offer a point of difference. With the bat, make sure they can whack sixes but also go down the gears when an innings starts to unravel. For an added trait, have them catch meteorites in the outfield and the cordon.

You might end up with Marco Jansen. At the start of the third Test, the 6ft 8in South African had taken 99 Test wickets at 20.81. His 85 against Australia at Gqeberha in the second Test came after South Africa had slumped to 110 for six before his counterattack helped turn a precarious position into an innings victory. Jansen is still developing as a batter, but his 25.66 average before this current Test understates his potential.

ICYMI, my learned friend Jack Snape scoured David Boon’s to-do list as the former Australia top-order batter puts memories of facing the West Indies’ bowling cartel behind him to now tackle the equally unenviable task of guiding the big ship that is Cricket Australia.

David Boon walked on to one of the stickier wickets in Australian sport on Wednesday, after Cricket Australia warned the national pastime faces years of financial losses and a period of “cost minimisation”. The outlook is grim, and that’s without a glance towards a cricketing world of emboldened match-fixers and upturned by Indian interests, facing an Australian summer that is no longer the country’s own.

The moustached former Test No 3 batter was sent into the middle due to the ousting of Mike Baird, whose place as chair was pulled out from under him by New South Wales officials unhappy at the manner of his pursuit of BBL private investment.

The runs are flowing once again in the ODI tri-series between England-Sri Lanka-Pakistan, this time with openers Ben Duckett and Tom Banton enjoying the flat deck at Lahore. We hope you don’t venture too far away, and not for more than another half hour, but do check in on the white-ball action over at …

An even session in keeping with much of this series. Australia added 81 runs while South Africa picked up four wickets including Josh Inglis (102) a couple of deliveries after he raised the bat for a century and Alex Carey (80) just as he looked well down the path to also reaching three figures. Simon Harmer claimed those two crucial wickets and he heads to the break with 4 for 104 from 37 overs as the Newlands deck shows signs of favouring the spinners. Cooper Connolly (20 not out) looked solid after a shaky start and was comfortable protecting the strike as Australia look to push their lead past 100 and perhaps well beyond.

117th over: Australia 411-8 (Connolly 20, Lyon 1) Lyon keeps Harmer out as South Africa crowd the bat. A maiden over and that’s lunch on day three.

116th over: Australia 411-8 (Connolly 20, Lyon 1) Coetzee keeps Connolly on strike as he spends half the over pitching the ball short and the rest sending it out wide. A maiden gives Harmer a shot at Lyon before lunch.

115th over: Australia 411-8 (Connolly 20, Lyon 1) Harmer gets the ball to straighten up and beat Connolly’s inside edge. The ball raps him on the pads and the South Africans are up in arms. But the umpire has little interest and Bavuma has even less in considering a review. A single to deep point from the fifth delivery helps keep Connolly on strike.

Cooper Connolly is doing all that he can with the bat at the moment. But he has been underused with the ball in his only two Tests with nine overs in South Africa’s first innings in Cape Town, and five overs on debut in Sri Lanka.

“Tuning in inbetween making lowball offers on marketplace – not sure of the logic of dropping one bit-part player in Webster, whose only real crime was to lack much opportunity, for another in Connolly, unless long term hes seen as a viable frontline spin option (which would make room for Boland),” Eamonn Maloney ponders. “What would you pay for a second hand set of bifold doors by the way? This guy’s dreamin’.”

114th over: Australia 410-8 (Connolly 19, Lyon 1) Connolly turns down an easy single as he is happy to face Coetzee and leave Lyon at the non-striker’s end. The South Africa quick overpitches with an attempted yorker and Connolly punches a drive through cover to the rope. He ends the over easing a single to deep point to maintain the strike.

113th over: Australia 405-8 (Connolly 14, Lyon 1) Lyon works the ball off his pads for a single to deep midwicket and Connolly adds another with a drive through cover. Dare I say, Connolly has looked quite comfortable against Harmer.

112th over: Australia 403-8 (Connolly 13, Lyon 1) Coetzee sends Starc on his way and South Africa are just a couple of wickets away from limiting what might have been serious damage to their hopes. Lyon gets off the mark with a glance. Connolly ends the over jabbing out a nasty yorker.

Coetzee gets his first as Starc stands tall and attempts to drive a delivery that pitches back of a length. A thick edge carries through to the keeper just as Starc looked as if he was about to get going.

111th over: Australia 401-7 (Connolly 12, Starc 11) Australia bring up the 400 as Starc clobbers a shorter ball through point and to the rope. He looks for the same stroke off Harmer again but is unable to pick the gap.

110th over: Australia 397-7 (Connolly 12, Starc 7) A better over from Coetzee as he finds his line and varies his length. Starc picks up a single as he steps back, opens the face and prods to deep point. Connolly has been patient but he can’t help to end the over taking a swipe at a full and wide delivery.

109th over: Australia 396-7 (Connolly 12, Starc 6) Connolly drives to long-off for a single as Starc picks up the same in less convincing fashion as he guides the ball wide of the cordon.

articles.title: Sri Lanka chasing 387 against England after Duckett century: men’s cricket tri-series one-day international – live
articles.summary: Updates from the final group match in Lahore Sign up for the Spin | And mail Daniel 1st over: England 0-0 (Banton 0, Duckett 0) Banton almost edges Asitha’s very first ball to slip, but it falls short. The ground is full only with empty green seats, as the call to prayer rings out. A maiden to start. The sun is out, Asitha Fernando has the ball, the drums are rolling. Continue reading...
articles.content:
No doubt if you’re into this, you’re also into this . Australia are rolling…

4th over: Sri Lanka 14-1 (Avishka 7, Kusal 1) Baker’s jib bears an appealing cut; he plays with attitude, moxie and skill. I think we’ll be seeing plenty of him over the next bit – in various formats.

REDEMPTION! As Peter Drury might’ve shrieked – or shrucked, were that the past participle. This is a terrific ball, hitting roud about a length and almost gathering speed, cramping Kamindu, who can’t sort out feet and hands quickly enough to stop it from rearranging his timber, done for pace.

4th over: Sri Lanka 13-0 (Kamindu 4, Avishka 7) Baker looked properly poorly with himself at that drop, so he charges in and nails an inswinging yorker that has Avishka hopping; he does well to jam down a bat and keep it out. He tries a similar delivery fourth ball and this time it’s nurdled into the on side for one.

3rd over: Sri Lanka 11-0 (Kamindu 4, Avishka 6) A wide, then a short one from Atkinson, so Avishka lifts one leg and briancharleslaras it around the corner for four. In comms, Nass chastises the length but, when England were batting, the Lankan bowlers were being chastised for being too full. Which tells us this track is a belter, with a pretty small area to hit to avoid being splattered. Anyhow, Avishka tries a similar shot to the one which brought him a boundary, cuthbertgordongreenidging to wide fine leg, if such a thing is linguistically possible, Baker runs, in dives forward, and will it carry? Just about, he gets both hands to it … and shells it, so they run one. Difficult chance, but once he got there he’ll feel he should’ve snaffled it.

2nd over: Sri Lanka 5-0 (Kamindu 4, Avishka 1) Sri Lanka will fancy this but, already into the final so perhaps not as focused in the field, they’ll need to find a bit more intensity with the bat. It’s Sonny Baker to open from the other end – I’m fairly sure Sam Curran and Henry Crocombe will also have fancied first shy – and in comms, Mark Wood makes the case for the former, partly because it means you don’t then have to finagle overs from him in the middle. I’d be especially wary of using him there in South Africa, where the World Cup mainly is, because at his pace he might just sit up pleading to be belted but, in the meantime, Avishka takes a single to third man, then deflects a delivery into his own elboid, a right sair yin.

1st over: Sri Lanka 4-0 (Kamindu 4, Avishka 0) Atkinson begins well, just outside off, and he’ll be wanting to use whatever movement there is while the ball’s young. Mendis, though, edges his third delivery for four – the only runs from the over.

In less affirming news, I’ve just opened a pack of pitot, planning to toast at least all of them to farshmeer with hummus and shito , only to discover they’re off.

It was touch and go, but you’ll all be relieved to learn I’ve got tomorrow night’s steaks dry brining in the fridge. Phew.

Otherwise, it’s been a funny tour for England: they’re 0-3, and yet there are loads of positives. The question now is whether they continue rotating the team or try and settle on an XI for the World Cup, starting in just under a year from now.

England are still looking for a win in this triangular tournament, but they will dine at the break confident (ish) that they’ve got enough for Sri Lanka this time, thanks to a tip-top 167 from Ben Duckett, his highest ODI score. The commentators think the batting conditions aren’t as easy as in the 800-plus game, but Nasser points out that there was no swing, no seam, other than in the first two overs. Perfect, he says with a grin, for a run chase. The dew is falling at Lahore, but I’m going to leave Daniel Harris to take you through to the close. Thanks for your messages, bye!

Arachchige lands with a thump on his back at long off, slipping while collecting Cox’s last-gasp throw of the bat from the final ball of the innings.

50th over: England 386-5 (Curran 21) With a six from Cox, England pass the highest ODI score at the Gaddafi stadium. Cox adds to the bounty next ball by shuffling to the off side and sweeping Madushanka for four, but that’s the last boundary and Cox falls looking for one more. England fall short of 400 but it is still an imposing total for Sri Lanka to chase.

49th over: England 372-4 (Cox 32, Curran 18) Eshan finds his mojo in his final over, which goes for just five runs.

48th over: England 367-4 (Cox 30, Curran 15) Asitha continues his parsimony into his tenth over, the first three balls going for singles, until Curran spoils the scoresheet, lofting him high …towards the boundary fielder …but he can’t hold on or keep it out and it drops over the rope for six. But figures of 2-63 pretty impressive in this onslaught.

47th over: England 356-4 (Cox 27, Curran 7) Curran plonks out his front foot and shovels a low full toss from Eshan down the ground. With one potential over left, he’s conceded 96.

46th over: England 345-3 (Cox 21, Curran 2) Clever bowling by Asitha first beats Jacks with a yorker and gets his prize the next ball. Root remains marooned between the muscle T-shirts of McCullum and a another coach, as Curran is sent in. Four singles follow.

Jacks drags a full ball from Asitha onto his stumps and kicks the bail in frustration as he heads home.

45th over: England 341-3 (Jacks 30, Cox 19) Jacks top edges Shanaka’s first ball for four, who follows up with a wide. His day gets worse when Pavan Rathnayake on the rope crouches into the long barrier but somehow misses and lets Cox’s pull trickle for four.

44th over: England 327-3 (Jacks 24, Cox 12) Cox, promoted above Root, joins the boundary gang, punching Eshan with pin-point precision between deep midwicket and long on.

43rd over: England 315-3 (Jacks 23, Cox 3) A wonderful innings that by Duckett, a man who has refound his touch. Shanaka runs in with over number six, Jacks flays him down the ground for four and next ball hauls him square past a hapless double act on the rope.

The stroke of a tired man, a slow low full toss blarghed to short fine where Asitha takes it on his knees. The end of a super innings.

41st over: England 298-2 (Duckett 166, Jacks 11) Just four singles in a clever over of varying pace from Shanaka, and a near run out as Duckett sends Jacks back. This is a career best now for Duckett, beatinging his 165 against Australia here during the Champions Trophy in 2025. A prize for anyone who can remember who won the competition.

40th over: England 294-2 (Duckett 164, Jacks 9) A woman with a gorgeous long black mane advertises shampoo in one of those live-action plugs. Duckett finds the gap off Asitha with another pull for four, and England jog five easy singles.

“A simply glorious day in Northern France, but the melancholy still clings to these flat fields and to the towns (Saint Quentin, Amiens etc).

“We’re off to bear witness at our great uncle’s stone, dead after three nights in no man’s land as a teenager in the mud and the blood.

“The names on the Menin Gate at Ypres appear like a list of Test Match statistics: English, Hindu and Muslim and everything in between. It’s a reminder that our forefathers fought alongside each other 110 years ago but now play alongside each other.

39th over: England 285-2 (Duckett 157, Jacks 7) Wellalage finishes his 10 over spell for a heart-shimmering 75. Fair play to Duckett, he’s shown excellent endurance and fitness both today and in the last match, still grinning after 39 overs as he sweeps Wellalage for yet another boundary.

38th over: England 277-2 (Duckett 151, Jacks 5 ) Brook is furious with himself, falling just after shimmying legside and nudging Asitha delightfully down to the rope. Jacks bumps Root further down the order and is off the mark with a Pietersenesque whip through midwicket. And Duckett brings up his 150 to enthusiastic applause.

From nowhere, Brook tries to flip Asitha over the keeper but gets in a pickle with his footwork and toe ends him instead back to a delighted Asitha.

37th over: England 265-1 (Duckett 148, Brook 40) Yes please says Duckett: pulls Wellalage for consecutive boundaries and then with a little nudge brings up the 100 partnership off just 70 balls.

36th over: England 252-1 (Duckett 136, Brook 39) Madushanka, towel tucked into his waistband, starts with three dots, but Duckett spots a wide slower ball and upper cuts it for four. He wipes his brow, I imagine he won’t be quite so game for quick singles in the last few overs.

35th over: England 247-1 (Duckett 131, Brook 39) Duckett dinks a full toss from Eshan Laminga over the keepers head for a very jolly four. Another boundary pulled with oiled joints. The crowd, which has grown, applaud sportingly. "Intrigued by your reply to TvdG (over 21) which suggested there would be a lot of ‘joshing’ for positions in the England team over the next 12 months,” writes Brian Withington. “I know the coach likes to operate a fairly relaxed regime, but didn’t think selection would resort to a Last One Laughing format - what’s next, Jimmy Carr as chair of selectors?” That would be a divisive choice even for Rob Key…

34th over: England 234-1 (Duckett 119, Brook 38) Madushanka waves his fielders into position, royal blue shirt tucked in neatly. Another one handed haul, a pull at a stretch, this time from Duckett, bounces just before the rope. England are cruising.

33rd over: England 224-1 (Duckett 112, Brook 35) Just a one-handed pull for six by Brook (almost into the hands of a diving fielder) and then four hauled through mid on. Eshan, elbows pumping, runs in again and Duckett – swivel and pull – sends him behind square for four more. Eighteen from the over.

32nd over: England 206-1 (Duckett 107, Brook 22) Brook has taken 22 balls to find his mojo but bang he hits the rope with a brutal sweep off Wellalage and next ball dispatches him out of the ground. He grins, ominously.

31st over: England 194-1 (Duckett 106, Brook 11) Are England eyeing up that 429 they pistolled against Sri Lanka about a week ago? Shanaka restricts England to three singles off the first three balls, but the fourth is slapped to the rope by Duckett. They all take a DRINK on a hot afternoon.

30th over: England 185-1 (Duckett 100, Brook 8) And there it is! With a gentle dab into the offside, back to back centuries, a sixth in ODIs, a third in Pakistan. He takes off his helmet, grins endearingly and wipes his perspiring forehead.

29th over: England 180-1 (Duckett 98, Brook 5) Shanaka keeps him hanging…

28th over: England 175-1 (Duckett 95, Brook 3) If Duckett gets to three figures, it will be his third hundred at Lahore in five games. A pull off Madushanka takes him a hit away.

Australia, by the way, have had a little collapse at Cape Town, despite Inglis’ century.

27th over: England 170-1 (Duckett 91, Brook 2) On TMS they’re banging the drum for triangular series. I agree, I do think they give context. I still remember the 86-87 tri series in Australia, when Allan Lamb conjured 18 from the last over off Bruce Reid to win England a game. Anyway, Sri Lanka review a caught behind decision off Brook, but lose the review as there was no bat involved. Another tight over from Shanaka until the last ball which allows Duckett to whip him off his pads for four.

26th over: England 165-1 (Duckett 87, Brook 1 ) Brook, double century fresh in his mind, gets off the mark with a dab down to third.

25th over: England 163-1 (Duckett 86, Brook 0 ) Shanaka replaces Wellalage and Banton, possibly frustrated by a couple of tighter overs by Sri Lanka, launches into an off cutter and plays on. Super innings and a perfect platform for Harry Brook, pushed up the order.

Banton, moustache decorating his top lip, not quite Burt Reynolds but getting there, drags on and bends over his bat in despair.

24th over: England 160-0 (Banton 72, Duckett 85) A fat pigeon lands on my neighbour’s crab apple tree and tucks into the red berries, rather like England, though they can only peck at Asitha this over.

23rd over: England 158-0 (Banton 71, Duckett 84) The strains of Despacito float over Lahore as some new gloves are brought out. And that is gorgeous, Banton gallops down and lofts Wellalage over long off for six, which is appreciated by the spectators who are scattered like confetti the day after a wedding.

22nd over: England 148-0 (Banton 63, Duckett 82) A kite flies across the pitch as Asitha bustles in. A super bit of fielding by Rathnayake at short mid wicket cuts off a brutal Duckett boundary.

articles.title: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse
articles.summary: Poundland's bosses is filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators to the business.
articles.content:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse, the BBC understands.

The retailer's bosses are filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which if approved by the High Court, will give the business 10 days breathing space to find a rescue deal.

The move comes after Poundland's managing director Barry Williams wrote a memo to his 12,000 staff across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland saying the chains' US owner had limited Poundland's access to funding.

It is understood the firm's owner, Gordon Brothers, wants to break up the firm, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up stores.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco in June last year for a nominal £1, but a little over a year later it put the business up for sale.

Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG) put forward a bid to take the business on as a going concern, which was the preferred option for management, but it is understood this did not meet Gordon Brothers' expectations.

Gordon Brothers wants to recoup a £30m shareholder loan it inherited from the previous owners as part of a its deal, but it is understood the Martin Property Group offer was for £5m, with the rest of the payment deferred.

Gordon Brothers could secure a new owner through what is known as a pre-pack administration.

But the most likely option for the business to be broken up and for parcels of stores to be sold.

Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.

It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.

The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis

A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.

If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.

These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores.

Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.

More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.

However, there is a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable".

"As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.

articles.title: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment
articles.summary: All but one of England's water companies were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement" for environmental targets.
articles.content:
The environmental performance of water companies fell again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.

Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.

Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".

The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".

"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".

Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.

It is a nod to the commitment which Sir Keir Starmer's government made to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation .

The Welsh government plans to set up a new regulator alongside Natural Resources Wales.

But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.

Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.

Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.

The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".

And in Wales, Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by Natural Resources Wales.

Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".

But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".

"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.

Water companies have committed record levels of investment up to 2030 to upgrade their networks and sewage treatment works. But customer bills are expected to rise 36% on average between 2025 and 2030 as a result.

There has already been £5bn invested over the last five years to try and tackle environmental pollution. But Lovell said "not all companies have delivered the environmental improvement schemes they have been funded for".

In September, it was reported that the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the Consumer Council for Water (CCW) rose by 84% in a year - the highest in 20 years.

Mike Keil, chief executive of the CCW, said that "many customers have not noticed any improvement in customer service or performance" despite recent bill rises.

"People support investment and understand it takes time to bear fruit," he said, but added that "bill payers are already questioning whether their money is being well spent."

The regulators said disruption to water supply was down but for some companies such as South East Water the levels remained "unacceptable"

The government is planning to introduce new legislation next year to overhaul the structure and regulation of the industry - including combining the England regulators.

In his Labour conference speech last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that a strengthened Water Bill would also remove limits on government ownership of shares in England's major water companies.

He also promised new powers for local leaders . The BBC understands further details on the idea of "regional bodies" to oversee water companies are likely to follow in the coming weeks.

The joint report, published on Thursday, also found that household consumption in England and Wales in 2025 remained similar to the previous year, at 137 litres per person per day.

Government advisers have said that people's demand for water will likely have to fall to safeguard future supplies , which are facing pressures from climate change, a growing population and historic underinvestment.

Hosepipe bans are in place across large parts of England and Wales this summer as companies have sought to shore up supplies during drought.

Mark Owen, head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said the industry needed to take more responsibility and cut leakage rates.

"After this summer, and the severe drought which we continue to experience, this failure to cut waste is indefensible.

"Every litre lost has already been taken from the environment while our rivers, fish and wildlife are under immense pressure."

Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?

articles.title: Mini-gardens for bees on bus stop roofs approved
articles.summary: Living Roofs aimed at boosting biodiversity in urban areas will be installed under a new bus stop contract.
articles.content:
Plans to introduce "bee bus stops" aimed to boost biodiversity in urban areas have been approved for Peterborough.

Peterborough City Council said 34 bus stops could include Living Roofs, mini-gardens planted on top of bus shelters that are made up of wildflowers and other vegetation.

The initiative was included in its new plan for the city's bus stops, which will also see "comfortable seating" replace existing perch seats.

At a meeting of the cabinet , external on Tuesday, the plans were discussed and approved.

The council will award a new contract to Bauer Media Outdoor UK to manage the city's bus stops.

The contract is expected to run for a minimum of 10 years, with options to extend it, and could provide the authority with £2.8m over 20 years.

There are more than 350 Living Roofs across the UK, including in Birmingham, Glasgow and Northampton.

Chris Wiggin, the council's Liberal Democrat cabinet member for environment, said: "We need to do everything we can to support biodiversity and support bees and other pollinators because without those there is no other life, so I'm very happy to see these [plans] come forward."

articles.title: England’s Ivan Toney to stand trial during Euro 2028 after denying assault charge
articles.summary: Striker’s trial due to begin on 12 June 2028 He has denied assaulting man at Soho nightclub Ivan Toney has in effect been ruled out of Euro 2028 after his trial for assault occasioning actual bodily harm was scheduled for 12 June 2028. Toney appeared at Southwark crown court and stood in the dock to confirm a not guilty plea. The striker is accused of head-butting and punching Saber Da Silva at a Soho nightclub on 6 December last year. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Ivan Toney has in effect been ruled out of Euro 2028 after his trial for assault occasioning actual bodily harm was scheduled for 12 June 2028.

Toney appeared at Southwark crown court and stood in the dock to confirm a not guilty plea. The striker is accused of head-butting and punching Saber Da Silva at a Soho nightclub on 6 December last year.

Setting the trial date for 20 months’ time, Judge Hehir apologised to Toney for the delay. “That’s a long way, I’m sorry about that,” he said. “As you may know, the crown courts are operating under a great deal of pressure.” Toney – wearing a black button-up cardigan, white shirt and tie – was told he was in a queue of defendants awaiting crown court trials.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Toney was part of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad for the 2026 World Cup, coming on against Argentina in the semi-final and starting the third-place playoff victory against France. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged by the Metropolitan police three weeks after the tournament. He was not part of Tuchel’s next squad for the Nations League fixtures at the end of September and early October.

It appears inconceivable the England manager would select a player for Euro 2028, which is due to be held in the UK and Ireland, while the player faces a criminal trial during the group stage.

Toney was released on unconditional bail and told it was “very important” and “a matter of common sense” that he stayed in regular contact with his solicitors while awaiting trial.

Judge Hehir told Toney that the law obliged him to give the footballer a formal warning, as with any defendant on bail awaiting trial, about the consequences of failing to attend court. “It’s a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment,” he said. The case would likely be tried in his absence if he did not appear, the judge added.

When Toney appeared at Westminster magistrates court to enter his plea at the start of October, the court was told by the prosecutor, Tom Heslop, that Toney and Da Silva exchanged words that resulted in them “squaring up” to one another before Toney “lunged forward and head-butted the complainant, followed by a few punches”. Da Silva sustained injuries to his nose and fingers, it was alleged. After pleading not guilty, Toney requested that his trial be heard at a crown court.

After the Metropolitan police announced Toney had been charged, a spokesperson for the player said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney, who has 10 England caps, started his career at Northampton before moving to Newcastle and Peterborough. His career took off at Brentford, where his goals helped them win promotion to the Premier League in 2021 before he established himself as one of the leading top-flight strikers. He moved to Al-Ahli for £40m in 2024.

articles.title: South West Water given lowest environmental rating
articles.summary: The water firm is performing "significantly below target" for pollution, the Environment Agency says.
articles.content:
Pollution from a treatment works killed thousands of fish in St Austell River last year

South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.

The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.

It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.

South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.

The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.

For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.

South West Water performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents

Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.

Industry regulator Ofwat said South West Water met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".

It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.

Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.

While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.

It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.

A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.

"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."

They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".

"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.

"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."

A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".

It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".

In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".

To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.

It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.
Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.
While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.
It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.
A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.
"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."
They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".
"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.

"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."

A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".
It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".
In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".

To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.

articles.title: Durban selected as South Africa’s candidate for Olympic bids in 2036 and 2040
articles.summary: Games would be first held in Africa if bid successful East-coast city preferred to Johannesburg and Cape Town South Africa on Thursday announced the east coast city of Durban as its preferred candidate to host the first Olympics in Africa. South Africa is bidding to host the 2036 or 2040 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. The International Olympic Committee will choose the host city for 2036 in mid-2029. Continue reading...
articles.content:
South Africa on Thursday announced the east coast city of Durban as its preferred candidate to host the first Olympics in Africa.

South Africa is bidding to host the 2036 or 2040 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. The International Olympic Committee will choose the host city for 2036 in mid-2029.

The country’s choice to put forward Durban, South Africa’s third biggest city, was announced by the South African Olympic committee’s acting president, Lwandile Simelane, who said Durban would be the main candidate city for her country’s bid, but it would probably be a “multi-city bid” that would propose some events are held in other cities.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

South Africa’s economic hub of Johannesburg and Cape Town were also considered as the candidate city.

Durban was touted as a possible Olympic host more than a decade ago after South Africa’s staging of the 2010 World Cup, the first in Africa. But an official bid did not materialise, largely due to concerns over costs.

Officials said on Thursday they were not yet able to provide any estimates regarding how much it might cost South Africa to stage the Olympics if its bid was successful.

South Africa is among seven countries bidding for the 2036 Games. The others are India, Qatar, South Korea, Germany, Hungary and Turkey.

The IOC gave 31 October as the deadline for national Olympic committees to formally declare their interest in bidding for those Games.

articles.title: A simple pub sign led me down a very disturbing rabbit hole
articles.summary: The cleanliness, or otherwise, of a pub’s pipes has never bothered me before. But that was before I read about the potential yeast, bacteria and mould ... There’s a pub near me with an eye-catching sign outside. I’ve driven past it many times, and it always gives me pause for a little idle thought. On the sign there is a loud and proud notice that in this pub they clean their lines every week. There’s a lot going on with this simple sign. First and foremost, in a long life of pub observance, I don’t recall ever reading such a boast adorning any other establishment. What’s going on here? Surely it’s not the case that this pub, and only this pub, is so scrupulous about the cleanliness of its lines. (By lines, I assume they refer to the pipes that convey the beer from the kegs or casks to the pump and into the glass.) Continue reading...
articles.content:
The cleanliness, or otherwise, of a pub’s pipes has never bothered me before. But that was before I read about the potential yeast, bacteria and mould ...

T here’s a pub near me with an eye-catching sign outside. I’ve driven past it many times, and it always gives me pause for a little idle thought. On the sign there is a loud and proud notice that in this pub they clean their lines every week.

There’s a lot going on with this simple sign. First and foremost, in a long life of pub observance, I don’t recall ever reading such a boast adorning any other establishment. What’s going on here? Surely it’s not the case that this pub, and only this pub, is so scrupulous about the cleanliness of its lines. (By lines, I assume they refer to the pipes that convey the beer from the kegs or casks to the pump and into the glass.)

Surely all pubs have a weekly flush-through? In which case, this sign is clever, but daft, making a virtue of a norm. Like a restaurant stating its chefs don’t sneeze on the food, or an airline assuring us that the planes’ wings are checked before every flight.

Always on the lookout for a fresh source of worry, I’ve been down a rabbit hole on the subject of beer line issues, and I’ve come up smelling not very nice. There’s a lot going on in those pipes – an awful lot if you’re not careful. Potentially, it’s hell in there. Living wild yeast and bacteria attaching itself to the interior of the tubes; mould around the taps and connectors; sticky protein residue left behind by the grain; and something called beerstone, a stubborn mineral scale that bonds to the plastic lining. Ye gods, it’s enough to put you off your beer.

I’m going to pop into this pub and suggest they clean daily instead of weekly. And as for every other pub I frequent, before I shout up a pint I’ll henceforth be asking for details of their line-cleaning regime. I may carry a hazmat suit to have a poke around in the cellar myself. You can’t be too careful.

articles.title: Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readings
articles.summary: Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination “This journey isn’t just about algorithms or data,” an AI psychic named Urban Mystic recently told me. The chatbot, featuring an AI-generated profile photo of a smiling woman surrounded by palm trees, also said I will get married soon, that I have a pink aura and that I may have been an herbalist in a past life. “It’s about connecting on a soulful level,” the chatbot said. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination

“This journey isn’t just about algorithms or data,” an AI psychic named Urban Mystic recently told me. The chatbot, featuring an AI-generated profile photo of a smiling woman surrounded by palm trees, also said I will get married soon, that I have a pink aura and that I may have been an herbalist in a past life.

Urban Mystic is one of more than a dozen bots on the mobile app Your AI Psychic, which offers live, allegedly psychic readings via chat, video and voice calls as well as palm reading, astrology chart analysis and daily horoscopes. The app works on a coin system: each question costs 4.06 coins to ask. Users can purchase packages ranging from $9.99 for “a quick question” (82 coins) to $99.99 (1,180 coins) for “ongoing guidance and clarity” from an AI psychic of their choice.

Your AI Psychic joins an increasingly crowded space of mobile apps and websites promising users algorithmically generated spiritual insight and knowledge of their futures. The divination industry, like mathematics research , copywriting, software engineering , and a host of other professions, is facing upheaval amid the AI boom – and human practitioners are scrambling to respond. The rise of AI is particularly fraught in a profession offering spiritual products that are not well-regulated.

“Our industry has, unfortunately, been associated with scams for hundreds of years, and we have to constantly be ahead of that,” said Lauryn Kellett, an intuitive coach and a professional psychic of 10 years. “So in some ways, this is not new to us: we always have to find ways to show we are real, authentic and have good integrity.”

In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views. Professional human psychics, who frequently make use of the social network’s live features, have expressed consternation and warned that computer-generated readings lack the empathy and human connection they say are central to psychic communication, especially Elon Musk’s Grok . Meanwhile, according to human spiritual practitioners , AI-generated horoscope readings and spells have been flooding Etsy, which serves as a popular marketplace for divination products.

Kellett, who coaches new practitioners on accessing their psychic abilities, said she has shifted her teaching toward how to best distinguish human-offered services from AI, as AI readings passed off as human work have become “rampant” online, encouraging clients to post videos and photos of themselves to prove they are not bots.

As the rise of users turning to AI chatbots for therapy underscores , many people feel more comfortable sharing personal problems with a faceless entity. But as with turning to AI for therapy, using AI psychics to process difficult situations may worsen mental health crises, practitioners warn. Studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can amplify paranoia in users vulnerable to psychosis. On TikTok Live, many human psychics, as a rule, refuse to answer questions about health or finances, arguing that high-stakes decisions should not be made in these contexts.

Ahna Hendrix is a psychic who, instead of channeling entities such as spirits from other realms, works with the Akashic Records – an extra-dimensional “database” of energy and human knowledge. She said her practice is centered on empowering clients rather than making decisions or recommendations for them – something that AI chatbots are less inclined to do.

“One of the cornerstones of my work is really helping people to remember who they are and to come back to their own internal guidance system that is within all of us,” she said. “When we begin leaning on AI too much for validation or for decision making, we stop using those mechanisms within us that are really important. If we start outsourcing that, what are we left with?”

A chatbot does not have to be branded as a psychic to serve a divination function, noted Sally Applin, a consultant and anthropologist who researches human agency, AI and automation in the context of human systems. People ask ChatGPT about life decisions such as whether to get a new job or leave their partner. In their book chapter, External Intelligence: Oracles, Divination and Animism, and the Use of LLMs/Generative AI, Applin and co-author Michael D Fischer argue that even prior to the explosion of LLMs, people turned to Google search with questions about their fates and choices.

“Some interaction with LLMs can be seen as a modern iteration of the oracular consultation,” they wrote. As with traditional divination, users must interpret the answers they receive, and sometimes ask the same question repeatedly until they are satisfied with the response. “The meaning is always coming from the inside of the person’s head,” Applin said.

Critically, however, she said LLMs work from statistical patterns learned in training and lack the cultural and personal context that historically inform human-led divinatory processes. The sense that a chatbot is a knowing entity is a projection of human expectations, she said, reflecting an enduring desire for connection and guidance rather than a metaphysical resource.

“What is also missing is contextual awareness, the ‘there there’ of human social relationships,” she said.

The models behind AI psychic chatbots offered on the app store are, as is often the case with LLMs, black boxes. One web and phone-based platform, MystiCall, markets itself as having been trained on “three generations of clairvoyants”. In a statement, co-founder Laurie-Anne Bernard said this wording refers to clairvoyance practiced in one of the co-founders’ families. The company also consulted with a human psychic who helped shape the app’s “conversational experience”.

Mysticall began as a human phone-reading service, but pivoted to AI as a means of “removing barriers” to such consultations, like cost and availability, Bernard said. The goal of Mysticall, Bernard added, is to offer a more accessible means of processing emotions through personalized consultations, not to offer explicit – and potentially harmful – predictions or mental health diagnoses.

“We do not claim that our technology possesses supernatural abilities or can reliably predict the future,” she said. “Instead, we see tarot, astrology and other symbolic traditions as ways of exploring questions, emotions and different perspectives. AI allows us to make these experiences more interactive, personalized and accessible.”

Kellett said this lack of transparency around how data is handled makes her particularly wary of AI apps. She said a number of platforms have contacted her for help training their LLMs, but when she pushes for more details, they tend to disappear.

Unlike many workers who fear they will someday be replaced by AI, Kellett said she does not believe her ability can be replicated by chatbots. Even if she were to hand over all of her training courses for developing psychic ability to an LLM, she does not think AI is yet at a point where it could make the leap to intuition.

“Psychic ability itself is the ability to connect to a divine source, and AI cannot do that,” she said. “AI can’t pull information from somewhere else. It can only derive information from what you give it. If you ask it to meditate, to sit down, to clear its mind, and connect to a psychic source, how would it do that? It’s just a computer.”

articles.content:
With a footprint of less than 40 sq metres, the Melbourne project required careful planning – and some spatial trickery

L ast week on a balmy spring evening, Ronnen Goren and his partner had dinner in a small pavilion on their terrace for the first time. Inside, an Aga stove was keeping their home warm. They could have retired to their sunken lounge room and cocktail bar for a nightcap, had the mood struck.

This domestic scene took place in a semi-subterranean former laundry in inner Melbourne – a space of less than 40 sq metres that was renovated at the end of 2024. On 29 October, the “exuberant” reimagining of the damp basement space in Toorak, on the grounds of the heritage-listed Quamby apartment complex, received the Emil Sodersten award for interior architecture at Australia’s National Architecture awards.

Originally designed as a service space by the acclaimed Australian architect Roy Grounds in 1941, its recent rebirth was overseen by Timothy Hill of Partners Hill. The project, titled Studio8, has transformed a poorly executed 1970s apartment conversion into an ambient retreat that belies its tiny footprint.

In 2022, despite the apartment’s “grim” condition, Goren says he and his partner were drawn to its “amazing location” and its “heritage and provenance”, not to mention the north-facing courtyard that’s almost bigger than the apartment. They lived in it as it was for about 18 months, “just imagining what it could be”.

That’s where Hill – whose interest in converting secondary spaces into quality housing stock dates back to his university days – came in.

“I saw it as a huge privilege, because I was able to run a sort of a test case,” Hill says. “Making little houses is a very particular sensibility. It’s not just squashed big. Every 25mm counts.”

When working with such a small internal footprint, Hill says some trickery is required. One of the bedroom walls is completely carpeted, while the living spaces feature other strategic sound absorbent materials: cork panelling is used for a feature wall in the living area while the upholstery is “gluttonously dense”, Hill says.

articles.content:
At Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes?

‘W e always say to the scare actors, you’re going to think the boys will be the worst. They are not.” Backstage at PrimEvil, billed as “Norfolk’s premier scare attraction”, park director Ben Francis is sharing the advice he gives each year to his new crop of performers, before they set out to give punters the fright of their lives – or at least their Saturday night. As Francis covers each demographic, he ticks them off on his fingers. Teenage boys “scream like banshees, and run in packs”. Teenage girls tend towards being unimpressed: “Do your scare and move on, because they will get nasty.” And mixed groups? “There will be an alpha and he’ll be wearing a North Face top.” Francis’s advice is to not waste time. “He will not react to anything … Aim for the weaker one at the back.”

This is part of the workplace induction at PrimEvil, one of many immersive “scream parks” that pop up across the UK in the lead up to Halloween . For about £40 a ticket, groups of all ages spend the night roaming themed attractions and being terrorised by actors and special effects. Though the risks are minimal, the spikes in heart rate are very real.

For Francis and the rest of the team, PrimEvil is months in the making. The nightly production involves more than 100 actors and dozens of crew, spread across six themed attractions, each drawing from familiar horror tropes – the scary clowns at the Circus of Terror, the cannibalistic trailer-dwellers over at Route 666, the satanic cult of The Offering. The winding routes are designed to disorient you with strobe lights, smoke machines, mirrored walls, hidden doors, false exits and unstable floors. But it’s down to the performers to bring the nightmare to life.

‘It’s the best form of therapy and you get paid to do it’ … park director Ben Francis

“I think people who don’t know what to expect think it’s just a nice little walk round, where you see the odd actor, they have a chat with you, then you carry on,” says Francis. “Actually, what the industry does now is completely immerse you in the theme of this world for 10 minutes.”

PrimEvil is the special Halloween event of ROARR!, a dinosaur-themed adventure park a half-hour drive from central Norwich. That family-friendly attraction remains open in the day during PrimEvil’s run. Now, coming up to 5pm, an hour before the gates open, the transition from theme park to scream park is under way.

It’s Saturday, the second night of PrimEvil’s nearly two-week run. Yesterday, 1,400 people spent the evening here, despite steady drizzle; the same number are expected later.

At PrimEvil HQ, a purpose-built warehouse, actors start flooding in for wardrobe and makeup. For our interview, Francis and I hole up in the laundry room, out of their way. Still, we’re intermittently interrupted by performers, partway through changing into costume, looking for plastic gloves or spray-on blood. Francis himself is in high demand, not just as PrimEvil’s boss of operations but also as an old hand. This is the 17th year he’s been involved, having attended the very first event in 2009. Though there were UK scare attractions then – notably Tulleys Shocktoberfest, now 30 years old, and Fright Night at Thorpe Park – they were still fringe.

Park life … a performer at PrimEvil takes a break from scaring punters

Francis didn’t know what to expect, he says. “I remember being absolutely terrified.” The following year, he applied to be an actor, and discovered a passion for scaring people. It’s not as sinister as it sounds, he insists. “It’s the best form of therapy, and you get paid to do it.” Francis was cast as a clown, “apart from one year where I was a hillbilly”. He found venting in character to be effective stress relief from his day job in the charities sector. “You shout at people, and they love it.” One evening in 2016, Francis arrived at PrimEvil in a foul mood after a board meeting had left him feeling disillusioned about his purpose. Martin Goymour, ROARR!’s founder and managing director, offered him a job. Both were in costume at the time, Francis confirms. “I was a clown, and he was in lederhosen.”

A familiar sight … Martin Goymour, ROARR!’s founder and managing director, dressed as Skullmore

Goymour joins us in the laundry room now, looking for face paint. We met earlier, at ROARR!’s offices across the park; I don’t immediately recognise him in his brocade suit and top hat, his face white and bloody. To PrimEvil regulars, Goymour is a familiar sight as “Skullmore”, the dark Victorian ringmaster, sweeping the park on his Segway.

Goymour was inspired to start PrimEvil in the mid-00s, after visiting Hollywood and one of Universal Studios’ legendary Halloween Horror events. The first PrimEvil, in 2009, was a single maze, built within the steel frame of ROARR!’s office building, after construction was paused by the recession. The idea was to draw a new crowd to the park after dark, and “have some fun” themselves. It was half a decade before the event broke even.

Now PrimEvil attracts 20,000 visitors annually (Tulleys, the largest in Europe, boasts 150,000), while most theme parks stage spooky-season events. Their popularity has grown alongside the mainstreaming of Halloween and horror in the UK, driving up the standard. There is even a trade show, ScareCON, and industry awards, the SCARs; PrimEvil won the top prize in 2024.

‘We say to the actors you can’t all be jump scares. You can be someone who just stands and stares …’

Francis and Goymour tweak the attractions every year and regularly travel to the US to scope out new tech and props. There, a single scare attraction can gross nearly $1m per season , though that’s offset by mounting costs. Goymour told me he spent “quite a bit” on “gory bodies” last year – about £10,000. According to IT manager Richard Colsell, responsible for the technical aspects of PrimEvil, the innovation is focused on electronic control systems. These trigger features such as animatronics or lighting changes; increasingly, the industry is using AI to read and respond to visitors in real-time, and even track their gaze.

Wherever possible, Colsell prefers to leave control in the hands of the actors. “Sometimes less is more.” With each performance typically lasting less than 30 seconds (then repeated for hours), theatrical chops are less important than dynamic range across the cast. “We say to the actors, ‘You can’t all be jump scares,’” Francis says. “That’s what gets the reaction, and the adrenaline – but actually, you can be a creeper scare, a stalker, someone who just stands and stares …”

‘More than once, catching someone’s eye, I’m startled by their red or white irises’

This year PrimEvil received an unprecedented 230 applications for about 132 paid spots. They were selected at a group audition, starting with a dance-off, then testing their improv skills. “The more of a prat you feel, the better you will be coming across,” says Francis. A self-avowed control freak, this year he “granted the gift” of assessment to his six team leaders, one for each attraction, who could also call dibs on performers. One man in his 70s was sought after by all six. “I had to shake a dice,” says Francis. The man wound up in Mayhem Manor, the haunted residential hospital where guests are chased by doctors and nurses wanting to violently uncover their “inner beauty”.

There are strict rules in place to protect actors and visitors, chiefly: no touching. Older women on a girls’ night can struggle with that one, says Francis. “They can get very touchy-feely.” Contracted security patrol the park for disruptive or intoxicated visitors. Performers are likewise instructed “no rude, lewd or crude” behaviour. People do strike out in terror, but actors are taught to distinguish between dodgy reflexes and ill intentions – and to watch visitors’ hands, which can suddenly spring up.

Still, accidents happen. “We have had code browns,” says Francis, though “not as often as you might think”. He estimates there are two each year, with more “code yellows”, though he assumes both are underreported. “Sometimes we’ll lend them trousers from our wardrobe, if they come and tell us.” Last night there were four panic attacks (about average, Francis says) plus two girls who fainted, and another who broke her finger. “She fell over while running away.” Most often, the on-site welfare team assists those wanting some quiet time-out.

‘My boyfriend kept jumping while watching Insidious, while I was literally taking notes’ … Courteney Dunn, head of makeup at PrimEvil

As Francis and I talk, actors emerge from the wardrobe transformed. A young man has traded his trackies for a boilersuit; there’s an increasing number of nuns. Francis admits to feeling a little wistful. “I used to love being a scare actor.” When he took the job at PrimEvil, nearly 10 years ago, he was “adamant” he wouldn’t give up performing. Now, due to the demands of his job as park director across ROARR!, he’s had to quit the Circus. His costume is still stored in wardrobe. From a wall lined with grotesque masks, Francis pulls down one with demonic arched eyebrows and crazed red curls, and introduces me to Lofty the clown: his longtime alter ego. “No one’s allowed to touch my clown costume,” he says, fingering the satin sleeve. He declines to don it for a photo – soon, it will be showtime.

Across the hall, the makeup team is finishing up the final few actors with brisk efficiency. Kara Field is applying brown and purple shadows to a Route 666 cannibal, to create sunken-looking eyes. “If you do it wrong, they look like drag queens,” she warns. Taped to the mirrors are print-outs with guide images and keywords for each attraction. This year the clowns’ makeup is monochrome for greater impact under the Circus’ UV lights. “We decided to go a lot darker, with more depth, shadows and contours,” says Courteney Dunn, 28, head of makeup and props.

Most of Dunn’s team of eight makeup artists are “obsessed” with horror. Watching the new Insidious film with her partner, “he kept jumping, while all I was doing was looking at the makeup, literally taking notes.” Where possible, makeup artists work with the actors’ style: unnatural hair colours or facial piercings might suit workers at the toxic Werehouse 51, but not the plague-time nuns of The Crypt. Dunn appraises me: “I feel like I could put you in Route 666.”

With 20 minutes before the gates open, actors are applying finishing touches to their looks, bloodying blond wigs or blackening their teeth. The scene is less nightmare than fever dream. There’s a nun, texting intently; two pilgrims at the sink, filling up their vapour-powered torches; a clown juggling a can of Monster, a vape and a sausage roll. More than once, catching someone’s eye, I’m startled by their red or white irises.

An estimated 50% of this year’s cast are returning, motivated by the experience as much as the work. “It’s a good way to make money, but it’s also really fun,” says Mia McConnell, 19, hanging out the front of the warehouse, vaping with friends. A shop worker by day, tonight McConnell is a mutant nurse. “The best way to scare people is to hide in the smoke. They don’t see you coming.” Sometimes the shock is mutual. Last night a trainee drama teacher (who requests anonymity) came face to face with some of her pupils, “super-excited to see Miss outside school,” she tells me, wincing beneath her bloody head bandages. Yesterday’s costume offered less coverage. “If I’d looked like this, I’d have been fine.”

‘It’s a good way to make money, but it’s also really fun’ … Mia McConnell in costume

A slowly clanging bell gathers everyone to the front of PrimEvil HQ for Goymour’s pre-curtain pep talk. In character as Skullmore, he greets his “children of the fright” and urges them to “speak up, entertain” – and stick to their assigned spots. Then, after a team chant of “PrimEvil”, the horde is released into the park, grabbing a fortifying Mars bar from the box Francis is shaking.

Scarlett Morris, 23, a barista and musician, is playing a ditzy sheriff at Route 666. In ordinary life, Morris tells me, she can be self-conscious and never leaves the house without makeup. “PrimEvil is the place to go to leave everything behind … it’s good for your confidence, dressing up and doing something you’d never do in real life.”

That might also explain the draw for punters. Research into “recreational fear” suggests it’s not just thrill-seeking but also a form of play, offering people a safe way to engage with difficult emotions. A 2025 study found that groups who went to a haunted house attraction reported feeling closer to each other, the “collective storytelling” solidifying their bonds.

For some actors it seems akin to a calling. This is Neville Everett’s 10th PrimEvil, and at the moment his only gig. “I’m a man of leisure,” he says, eyes mischievous beneath his evil-clown makeup. Everett sticks largely to the same playbook, loitering by the Circus’s exit and jumping out just when people think they’re safe. “Then I chase them,” he says. Usually he has a chainsaw going.

He struggles to articulate the precise appeal. “It’s just something I like doing … You get rid of your frustrations on people.”

Watching Everett in action, however, this sells him short: his dance with the public seems both conscious and two-way. A group of teenage girls literally plead for his attention (“Hi! Hi! Shalom!”), squealing in delight when he duly revs his chainsaw. When a pair of boys pass by, studiedly aloof and above the game, Everett calls their bluff and ignores them; they can’t hide their disappointment.

Judging by the screams coming from the nearby Werehouse 51 and the whacks reverberating along the corrugated-iron walls, PrimEvil is in full flow. In the now-quiet warehouse HQ, Francis settles in for the late evening, keeping things ticking over until the gates close at 11pm, and beyond. One of his tasks is doing “constant” loads of laundry, washing and drying the black bags that go over visitors’ heads for The Offering.

For all the hard work that goes into designing a frightening night out, ultimately it’s all about the visitors’ imaginations, Francis says. A sign hangs in his office, gifted to him by Goymour: “The biggest fear is the fear of the unknown.”
