Here, a senior official played a WhatsApp voice message in which Arian encouraged some of the students not to lose hope, to motivate them. He accused Arian of working with infidels, being a puppet of the west and “an apostate”. He insulted his appearance. Then he spoke to the tall Talib, saying: “Let’s teach him.”

The tall young man blindfolded Arian and led him through a long hallway, down about two floors and into a basement room. He tied Arian’s hands. Arian could hear that two or three others were there. They spoke in Pashto: “His excellency says we must teach him a lesson.” They called him “an infidel”, and “a dog”. Something hard struck his nose and jaw – he realised it was the butt of a rifle – and he was kicked until he lost consciousness.

He came to, lying in a lot of blood. One of his fingers was broken, his upper body was beaten and his nose and jaw were badly injured. He asked to have his blindfold removed and his hands untied, which a different man did. He was in a small and very dirty cell.

A rian was born in 1997, in rural Afghanistan, near the border with Iran, into a community already broken by the Soviet invasion in 1979 and the civil war that erupted after it left in 1989. His father – a tailor – had a talent for maths, but only had a few years of primary education and wanted something better for his son. “My dreams began because of my father’s belief in me,” says Arian.

He remembers the excitement of walking with his cousins to the village’s first school, on the day it opened in 2003. There were no buildings, just tents, which – like the books, pencils, even the biscuits they were given at break – were all provided by the United Nations Children’s Fund.

There were landmines buried for miles across this dry, sandy region. The wind carried dust – some days, they could barely see a metre in front of their faces. Every few weeks a schoolmate gathering firewood or a mother fetching water would step on a mine and lose a leg or an arm, or sometimes, says Arian: “There was nothing left to save.”

There was not enough rainfall to grow much, although people kept trying. When he was about 10, for the first time, Arian saw a rose that someone had brought from the city. Drinking water came from a spring, and Arian walked for miles with his father and their donkey to fetch it. Once, they saw the distant shape of an aeroplane in the sky, and Arian’s father pointed upwards and said to his young son: “One day, you’ll travel in one of those.”

His family were poor but, unusually, their home had books, which Arian’s father ordered from Iran or brought from the city. Arian read Robinson Crusoe and The Little Prince, and his father introduced him to classical Persian poetry. He passed every exam with top marks, but people laughed at his father’s belief in education, and thought it unrealistic. By the time he was 15, Arian was the only student left in his class.

In 2012, he left his village to continue his schooling in Herat. His new classroom had walls, desks and chairs, and better trained teachers, but he worried about being teased for his country accent. Two years later, he was the first person from his area to be admitted to the engineering faculty at Herat University. “My parents were overjoyed,” he says. The family moved so that his siblings and cousins could keep studying as well.

When he started university, Arian was skinny and fragile, and he began going to the gym. “The gym was my therapy,” he says. He read hungrily, to try to understand the situation in his country. He noticed newer versions of “political Islam”, which were “hostile towards women”. He went to poetry readings, took part in debates and spoke on local television about social issues, corruption and human rights. He became well known locally, and started to get threats from various religious groups. “I was not alone,” he says, but “part of a network of brave men and women.”

In 2017, he graduated and was keen to help rebuild the country. The following year, he was in a taxi in Kabul, looking for work, when a suicide bomber exploded his device 100 metres away. The blast wave caused a cloud of dust, smoke and body parts to hit the car windows and the smell was terrible. Arian’s ears were ringing as the taxi driver reversed away from the explosion. He was deeply shocked and it dawned on him how very hard it was to respond with logic to that sort of violence. “All of a sudden, you can be wiped out,” he says.

In 2019, Arian was elected as a youth representative to the Loya Jirga, a traditional assembly of political, community and religious leaders called upon at critical points in Afghanistan’s history to debate issues of national importance. Here, he saw the division and mistrust between urban professionals with smartphones and men from remote rural areas with very traditional dress and beliefs. By the time he took part in a second Loya Jirga in 2020, the country was on the verge of collapse. The US had withdrawn most of its troops: Arian says he could guess “the end of this story”.

More people were coming to the city, displaced by fighting and the climate crisis, and Arian decided to study for a master’s in urban planning over the border in Iran. He was home on a visit in August 2021, when Afghanistan finally fell to the Taliban. Arian felt that the world had abandoned them. It was like watching a building collapse, he says, or “like an emotional breakdown”. His mother cried a lot, because she had lived through the first Taliban era (which had ended in 2001, after the US invasion). Arian and his friends stayed awake all night, in shock, exchanging messages and going through their social media accounts, hiding content that put them at risk.

Women stopped being seen in public. The city was flooded with Taliban fighters, roaring around on motorbikes or crammed into military vehicles they had captured, celebrating with flags and songs. It was surreal and frightening: many had never been to a city before, and wanted to try ice-cream and pizza, but Arian knew they could kill without hesitation. His friends exchanged hushed news of raids, revenge killings and disappearances.

Arian’s sister was in secondary school. A few weeks later, the driver of the vehicle that normally collected her from the end of the road said that girls were no longer allowed. Arian saw her standing in her uniform with her schoolbag, crying. She wanted to become a doctor.

I n May 2022, Arian had to return to Afghanistan to renew his visa. It was during this visit that he received the call from the Talib official to come to the intelligence directorate. After he awoke in the cell, he was given bread and water, and was told he could pray. He objected, saying that in Islam it is forbidden to pray with blood on your clothes. He couldn’t sleep, thinking about his mother, suffering from his injuries, and worrying that his face would be disfigured. Before dawn, he was taken to a washroom and again told to pray, which he did. When he touched his face, it was in spasm.

In the morning, he was once again blindfolded, and taken back up to the same office as before, where he was forced to sign a statement saying that he was sorry, and warned not to talk about it, or he would be killed. He got his phone, was released, and took a tuk-tuk to the hospital.

An X-ray showed that his nose was broken in four places and his jaw was broken. The doctor had to wait a few weeks for Arian’s face to heal a little before he could operate on his jaw. After that, he had surgery on his nose, before returning to Iran as soon as he could.

He didn’t want “to let the girls down”, so he tried to keep the online classes going with the help of a volunteer, but stopped any new recruitment. His face healed, but he was “mentally devastated”, and struggled to recover. “It was just not fair. I couldn’t forgive them,” he says. After about a month, he was able to return to the gym, which helped him unwind. He finished his dissertation and graduated.

He wasn’t allowed to work in Iran and was on the verge of homelessness when he applied for a Chevening scholarship – a prestigious, fully funded chance to study for a one-year master’s degree in the UK. It was a long, complex and competitive process, followed by a two-hour visa interview. Against the odds, he won a place to study international development at the Institute of Development Studies based at the University of Sussex. He flew from Tehran in September 2024. As the plane descended towards Gatwick, he thought of his father’s prediction, years before. He was worried he might be stopped, but the woman at passport control smiled and said: “Welcome to the UK!”

His new life was not easy. Some international students on his course were hostile and made racist comments about Afghans. “I did not expect the sense of isolation I sometimes felt,” he says. Arian gave an interview on BBC Persian criticising the Taliban’s policies. When the course ended, most other students flew home, happy and proud, with gifts for their families. Arian had nowhere to go. Returning, especially after the BBC interview, could mean death. Applying for asylum was not something he chose freely, he says, but was “a decision that reality forced upon me”.

He arrived at the Home Office in Croydon with only a few pounds left. They asked lots of questions and told him to call a helpline and ask for urgent accommodation. He phoned again and again, but, he says: “They just said someone will call you, send this or that document.” He was homeless for six days, spending the nights in a park, and the days in Starbucks, where he charged his phone.

Then he was told to go to Croydon police station, where a taxi picked him up. Two women, one from China, the other from Hong Kong, were already in it. The driver told them they were heading for Liverpool. The only thing Arian knew about Liverpool was the football team.

He was taken to an asylum hotel, arriving late at night. The staff were kind, but it felt “like being in detention”. Everyone was traumatised and depressed. There was not enough food, and what was available was terrible quality – Arian lost weight, couldn’t sleep and felt very low. There were other Afghans “all fleeing from torture by the Taliban”, some because of their beliefs or ethnicity, some because they had served in the previous regime. There were also Iranians and refugees from other conflicts. Sometimes, they were warned to stay inside, because of the risk of protests. They got £1.30 a day and were not allowed to work.

Arian didn’t have a solicitor and knew little about the asylum process, but handled it himself, researching online. It was stressful, but swift compared with others in the hotel. He had an interview in October 2025, and a couple of days later got an email granting him refugee status. He left the hotel after two months.

After four months volunteering at a construction company to get UK experience, Arian got his first paid job as a civil engineer this summer. He is also translating into Farsi The Places in Between, a book about Afghanistan by Rory Stewart. He is grateful to be safe, and for the support he has had, and is excited about working and contributing to this country. He says the media are often “wrong and unjust” on these issues. “Migrants are the most defenceless group, and some politicians pin every problem on them. It’s not fair to reduce millions of people to a single threatening cliche.”

Arian rejects the idea that suffering “makes you stronger”, and says that some experiences just take things away from you. He has a sense of how fragile life can be, and doesn’t take stability for granted: “You start preparing yourself, almost automatically, for the worst.” He says his own life hasn’t given him confidence in a happy ending.

His father’s belief that a better future was possible, which he says he absorbed as a child, helped him to keep going. Reading and studying were always important to him, and he writes a lot of lists to instil a sense of order. Going to the gym has been crucial, especially when other parts of his life felt stuck or out of control. And “human connection really matters”, he says, including the random pleasant interactions which, in a new country, can make such a difference. All these things help him find the strength to move forward.

The impact of the torture stayed with him long after his physical injuries had healed. He says it was a feeling of violation, of having his dignity and control taken away: “Coming to terms with the fact that someone chose to do that was very difficult.” For him, recovery is about “finding a way to live with what happened, without allowing it to take over”.

He can’t forget the realities for so many people still in Afghanistan, especially women, without education, healthcare or other basic freedoms. In March, the UK government introduced a temporary ban on study visas for all Afghans, so, for now, the route he took is barred. It is a heavy burden – trying to use his voice and do the best he can with the opportunities he has, but also to be realistic about what he can’t change.
His message for other refugees is to “hold on to your human dignity”. He says it’s possible to “come out of even the deepest darkness, as I did”.

articles.content:
Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch This piece first appeared in the Dial

‘Hello Professor Snigdha Poonam,” the email began. I read that again. Nobody has ever called me “professor” for the obvious reason that I am not a professor. Bracing myself, I read on. The email was from Timothy Firth, organiser of a Seattle-based life-drawing community with 1,943 members that regularly has “thoughtful discussions inspired by creative works”. A recent inspiration was my first book, Dreamers: How Young Indians Are Changing Their World . The group wanted to discuss it, the email said, at one of its upcoming meetups. Attendees would be encouraged to post reviews on Goodreads and Amazon after.

I looked up CAM Life Drawing and found an events page and an Instagram account. The latter had some photos of Timothy Firth – white, male – as well as testimonials from members who said he worked “day and night to create more community space”. Something told me this wasn’t the man who had reached out to me.

Why would a hyperlocal life-drawing community in Seattle be interested in a nonfiction book about the shifting aspirations of young people in India’s small towns? The book was published seven years ago. What did they want from me?

I accepted the invitation. The next email had a slick poster promoting the Zoom event, with the book cover as the backdrop and blurbs from the Economist and other publications. My attention was drawn to something more intriguing: a request for a “contribution fee”, with no amount specified. It would cover promotion, coordination and administration. But, oddly, this email didn’t come from Timothy. Signing off this time was Stephen – “Organiser, Community Improv LA”, which was another group in another city. According to the improv community’s Facebook group, Stephen is indeed the name of the organiser. However, Stephen had written to me using Timothy’s email address. To add to the chaos, Stephen/Timothy had also left what I suspect was an AI prompt in the email, which included the line: “MAKE IT MORE PROFESSIONAL.”

This was undoubtedly a scam. Genuine book clubs don’t ask for money from authors. But who was behind it?

Had these individuals actually read my work, they would have wanted to stay away from me. I have spent the last 10 years reporting on transnational fraud. My first book, Dreamers, closed with a chapter on fake call centres in India; my second, Scamlands, travelled to other low-income countries in Asia to portray an invisible empire that thrives on inequality, technological change and the erosion of trust.

Along the way, I met and interviewed the scammers whose labour keeps this empire running. For some, fraud was a route to upward mobility; for others, an act of revenge against the privileged. Though I have formally emerged from this underworld, I can never delete a scam email without wanting to know more.

I agreed to pay the book club – but after rather than before the event. After clarifying that “Stephen” was a typing error, “Timothy” sent me a Google Meet link for the book discussion. I joined the meeting to find about 20 people already in there: Alexander, Andrew, Mira, Rajnish, another Alexander, and several others. Timothy was also there and so was Stephen. None of them had their cameras on. Going by the profile pictures they used, most of them appeared to be white.

“Professor, what did you learn while reporting from Indian small towns?”

While the questions may have been AI-generated, the voices seemed human. They did not always align with their pictures. Timothy seemed to be a woman, not a man, judging by the voice. Who were these people? They left only one clue. All these ostensibly white people, men and women, spoke with a west African accent.

I am not the only author to have found myself stuck in a Zoom book club with fake readers. Countless writers with published books have been receiving invitations from reading communities that start to unravel after a basic Google search.

As often happens with scams, most invitations sound too good to be true – thousands of members, incredible Goodreads clout and, at times, something even more alluring for an author: a deep understanding of their book.

One author who engaged with a book-club impersonator was told a $100 (£75) contribution for the online event would cover snacks for the participants; she withdrew without asking how they would partake of the snacks while on Zoom. Novelist Marsh Rose, playing along, exchanged 29 emails with the Chicago LGBTQ Book Club. “The individuals whose voices I heard on the Zoom didn’t seem to be speaking from Chicago. They all sounded like my friend in Nigeria,” she wrote in a blog post for WritersWeekly.com, an online resource for authors that offers writing opportunities and industry news.

Writers are also being bombarded with offers to publish our next book, market our book, handle social media for us, represent us as agents and get us book-to-movie deals with Netflix and Paramount. Every major publisher, agent, editor, author union and literary award executive is at risk of being impersonated.

The money requested often seems small. “Amounts reported to me range from $55 to $350. In one case, the scammer offered three ‘spotlight packages’ – basic, essential and premium – for between $100 and $200,” Victoria Strauss, co-founder of Writer Beware, an anti-scam watchdog, wrote in a blog post. Often, the paper trail leads to Nigerian third parties holding bank accounts in the US. Author Jon Cocks paid $478.65 to one “Mary Brown ,” who claimed a wide network of book clubs across the US, the UK and Australia, only to later notice the name Dayo Oguntuase listed as the recipient on the PayPal statement.

The Writers’ Guild of Great Britain (WGGB) reports “an explosion” in the number of members seeking advice about unusually enticing offers in recent months. “Even the most vigilant of writers are understandably falling prey to these scams,” WGGB’s general secretary, Ellie Piers, said in a statement commenting on new guidance, co-issued with the Society of Authors in May, to help authors protect themselves against scammers. “Our advisory team receives at least a dozen reports of scams each week,” Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors, said in her own statement, tracing the spike to the emergence of generative AI. The US Authors Guild says it hears from authors who have been scammed, or nearly scammed, every day. Angela Hoy, the founder of WritersWeekly.com, told me she is in touch with “authors all day long, every day, thinking they got an offer from one of the top five publishers in New York or thinking they’ve been contacted by a famous literary agent”.

The scale of the operation became clear after US authorities launched an investigation into the business. According to the Department of Justice, more than 800 authors were defrauded of upwards of $48m (£36m). Writer Beware received hundreds of complaints about PageTurner. One author reportedly lost more than $600,000 (£450,000). The prosecutors found that at least $42m in proceeds were laundered through accounts in the Philippines. One defendant pleaded guilty in May of this year, while three others are awaiting trial.

Judging by the surge in both the number and range of baits used on authors over the past couple of years, the scams seem to be launched from multiple territories. Anyone who has researched publishing would know most authors don’t have bundles of cash lying around. So why are the scammers coming after us?

Hoy, who has dealt with thousands of writers at WritersWeekly.com, puts it down to ego. Brian Whiddon, the site’s managing editor, elaborated: “Not every author is a narcissist, but they all want to be recognised. That’s exactly what these scammers are targeting. They have identified a very, very lucrative niche.”

Writers are waiting “for somebody to read their writing”, Hoy added. She argued that is why many writers believe the praise scammers heap on them. AI makes many of the compliments sound nuanced and personalised. Elderly authors are particularly vulnerable. As Hoy explained, a significant number of people who have a book in them leave off the writing until they have retired. Something else also kicks into the picture at this life stage: a sizable retirement fund. Scammers know American people have worked their whole lives and have retirement accounts, Hoy said.

Some authors are so hell-bent on signing up for the deals the scammers promise that they disregard Hoy’s counsel. Others come to Hoy when it’s too late. She has said one of the writers in her community paid more than $100,000 for a fake book-to-movie deal.

Even as a new category of literary scams emerges every few days, authors have very little information about the people behind them.

In August, Danny de Hek, a New Zealand-based scam buster, forwarded me an Excel spreadsheet he received from a scammer in Karachi, Pakistan , with permission from the sender. Titled “LinkedIn Outreach 2026”, it has monthly data on targeted authors from March until August. One sheet has 403 names, each neatly labelled: new author, cookbook author, religious author, investigative author, poetry author, New York Times bestselling author and so on. Most are based in the US; the rest are in Canada, Australia or Europe.

It’s an incredibly detailed document, with columns for the name of the person who found the profile, the person who first reached out, the service the author needs (website development, illustrator, social media visibility), the department handling the author, meeting links shared with the author. In a few cases, the document also lists the outcome of the outreach.

“Meeting booked Wed 12 Aug, 10pm PKT, number confirmed, deep trust-built relationship, ready to invest, needs custom package built around limited budget and multi-project scope.”

Some of the details only make sense if you know the context. 10pm PKT would mean 10am on the US west coast and 1pm in the east. Danny told me that most of the people working on this scam are Pakistani, yet the names of the callers are all American-sounding – Ashley, Jocelyn, Megan – probably to fool the authors into thinking they are Americans working for US-based companies and groups.

Scam recipients often find the emails they receive haphazard and random. But the modern scam industry is a highly organised system modelled on the global corporate setup, with clearly laid out deliverables, salaries, incentives and reporting structures. Even though the schemes are mind-boggling in range, the young people joining these “companies” are given the same targets: Americans on top, followed by gullible foreigners in other western countries. I spent several years reporting from India on its massive scam call-centre network, which employs hundreds of thousands of educated young people trying to beat the dim economic prospects offered by the domestic labour market. Similar Excel spreadsheets are used to organise schemes where Indian scammers in Delhi or Kolkata impersonate Microsoft tech support, the Internal Revenue Service or even the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

De Hek, who exposes transnational scams on his blog and YouTube channel with relentless zeal, told me Pakistan’s fake companies offering literary services operate in a similar fashion to India’s scam call centres. The majority of them maintain physical offices in Karachi and Lahore and employ people aged 20 to 24. Upon joining, the young employees typically get assigned to a unit, each designed around a specific literary swindle. While entry-level employees may only be tasked with outreach, the more experienced ones are entrusted with building long-term relationships aimed at selling multiple “packages” to clients over months and sometimes years.

The most profitable service targets authors lurking outside the notoriously gatekept realm of traditional publishing. Rather than through a cold call or email, the scammers lure them through websites offering self-publishing or vanity publishing.

Scam companies in Pakistan trap writers by impersonating known publishing houses and paying thousands of dollars to influence search results on Google. As a result, someone with a finished manuscript who searches online may find sites such as penguinwriters.com or amazonglobalpublishers.com before any legitimate self-publishing platform. Unlike traditional publishing websites, these feature open calls for new writers. WritersWeekly.com estimates there are at least 3,000 such sites. The biggest tell: a chat box pops up in the bottom right of all fake publishing websites as soon as the page opens, followed by a message from someone with an American-sounding name (such as Mark Anderson or Jessica Parker) and a white person’s face: “How can I help you today?” “Talk to a live agent, not a bot!” claims a ticker. And that much is absolutely true: the person messaging you is a scammer whose shift is dictated by the waking hours in your time zone.

None of the five major trade publishers has sued alleged impersonators. The only recorded instance involves Amazon, which took nearly 20 individuals and associated companies to court in California for falsely claiming affiliation with Amazon Publishing and Kindle Direct Publishing to deceive authors. Amazon won $36.4m (£27m) in February 2025.

M L Stark, a Danish self-published author of several psychological thrillers, is one of the rare victims who has met – and confronted – her scammer in person. Last year, she flew to Thailand to meet with Ethan Williams, a man she believed had become her longtime editor at an LA-based self-publishing house affiliated with Amazon – and a close friend. By this time, she had been talking to him over Zoom and email for more than a year and paid his company about $100,000 for different author services, from editing and cover design to coverage in the New York Times and the Los Angeles Times .

While most of the services she paid for never materialised, the company did follow through on some. They signed her up on IngramSpark, a self-publishing platform, which enabled her to release two books, and Amazon, which made the books available on the platform. Most notably, in 2024, one of her titles was displayed on a digital billboard in Times Square.

“I had paid $10,000 for that,” she told me. Only later, she told me, did she come to see these deliveries as strategic concessions, held back for moments when a long-term client reached the end of her tether. “Each time, it happened when I told them, after months of them stalling, that I wanted my money back.”

The scammers’ last pitch was a Netflix adaptation that they claimed the film-makers wanted to shoot in Thailand – an important setting in her upcoming book, a thriller based on her own life. Stark and Williams were meeting in Thailand to scout locations.

He had told her he was a British citizen, half English and half Arab; as a light-skinned Pakistani, his story was plausible. “He is an artist, he knew how to play the role,” she said. Still, she asked him to show an ID. He produced one that looked clearly faked. “I demanded he show me his passport,” she said. That exposed his real name and citizenship. He came clean. “He said, ‘Yeah, this has been a scam from the beginning. Even Peter is using a fake name; even Ronald is using a fake name. Everybody in the company that you have talked to is a scammer. It’s a huge scam operation, and we are not based in Los Angeles. We are based in Karachi.’” She is still processing her shock.

I clicked on a random website from a list of known scam sites; it happened to be impersonating Red Rock, a real literary agency based in London whose authors have been published by major publishers such as Hurst, which published my first book in the UK. Bold promises greeted me on the homepage.

A chat window opened, and someone with the username “Rae Donnaelly” asked how she could help. I told her I had an idea for a book. She asked for my contact, then called me on WhatsApp from a US number. She spoke like a South Asian imitating an American accent, something I could easily recognise because I’m South Asian myself, and we’ve all tried it at one point or another.

I told her the truth: I was writing an article about author-baiting scams, and I was hoping she could tell me about her experience working for a fake publishing house.

She told me she wasn’t “authorised” to talk about the company she works for, and she refused to tell me her real name. But she had no qualms spilling the beans on her ex-employer.

Rae has a law degree but found it difficult to find a job in law after university. Her first job after graduating was at a fake publishing company in Karachi. “I started working for a company which was a scam – a guaranteed scam – and I didn’t know it when I started off with them. I was an intern trying to learn how the system really works; what the pros and cons are.”

It took Rae only a few days to figure out the company’s business model: proxy sales. They would tell the author they would get them a guaranteed sale order for 1,000 copies, or something like that, making “fake commitments”. The scam rarely stopped there. After a client signed up for developmental editing, they would be offered a discount on book-cover design, and once they paid for that, the scammer would dangle social media management. “It could start off from as little as $400- $500, and it could go up to the skies, like $10,000, $15,000.”

As with all scams, those executing the con learned how easily people can be manipulated if you know what they desired. “You could see how the human brain works. It’s actually scary when you think about it,” Rae admitted.

She believes Americans make easy scam targets. “People in the US are very nice, they’re very good-hearted people. They trust you. Whatever you’re saying, they trust you. That’s the problem.”

At times, the clients only noticed they had been scammed after they had paid all the way up to a Times Square display and Broadway adaptation. “When the authors did not see results, they would either reverse the charge on their card or accuse us of being scamsters,” Rae recalled.

According to Talal Choudhary, an Islamabad-based tech journalist, there are about 1,000 Pakistani companies running scam sites. “One company runs as many as 25 websites. I personally know a company that had about 200 employees, just offering services to writers.” These companies are “very, very profitable”, he said. “From one client, you can make $60,000.”

In Pakistan, Choudhary told me, the workforce of the author-baiting scams is largely made up of high-school and university graduates. They earn an average salary of about 50,000 Pakistani rupees (£136) a month. For high performers, there is commission. For every sale worth $1,000, they might get a 10-20% commission, he said, upselling until the author backs out.

According to Rae, any guilt the scammers felt was cancelled out by the increasingly skewed conversion rate between the American dollar and Pakistani rupee. “Generally, the mentality was: when you’re making income in dollars, you have a stable life, you have sustainability. So that’s what they did. They just ripped people off.”

I have heard multiple versions of this statement since I first reported on the rise of organised transnational fraud. Earlier this year, Hoy received a message on Facebook from a Nigerian man who offered to market her latest novel. Convinced he was part of the suspected author-scam network, she made him an offer of her own: write an article for Writersweekly.com about how the company he worked for scams Americans while being based overseas.

But he wrote it using AI, which is against the site’s submission rules. He also ignored the brief. Instead, he chose to highlight, as Hoy recalls, “how it’s so hard for people in Africa and therefore it’s OK to scam Americans because all of us are rich over here”.

Salil Mahmood, who asked that I change his name, is another self-described ex-scammer from Karachi. He reached out to me after hearing from Danny de Hek about the article I was writing. Compared with some of the more outrageous deals his seniors offered their clients, his job, as an entry-level recruit, was low-key. He cold-emailed published authors with a proposal to create their official pages on Wikipedia and have those approved. However, many of the pages he created – largely based on information provided by the authors – failed verification because the citations he supplied were fabricated. “The pages would remain active for a while and then disappear.” The authors never got their money back.

While he only worked there for a few months, he said the setup was highly aspirational for those who wanted to make serious money. “The bosses would show us pictures of their lifestyles: mansions, fast cars, parties and lots of alcohol. If you met your targets, they would have a rented car drive you around.” But in keeping with the nature of such enterprises, failure was not an option. “If an employee did not meet the target, they and their families were threatened with violence,” he said.

Rae left the company she had been working for after a disagreement with her manager less than a year into the job. But rather than go back on the job market, she and a few friends started a new company that, as she described, provides American authors with tailored services.

She insisted her company did not defraud its clients. I could have asked her why, if it was a genuine publishing house in Pakistan, it gave clients the impression that it was based in the US; why the website featured books it had not published; or why the individuals who popped up in the chat boxes used fake, American-sounding names, including her. But I left it at that. I could sense she wanted me to believe she had nothing to do with the scammers. She even pointed out that her religion does not allow her to earn money from fraud.

“You can look out for us at the next Frankfurt book fair,” she said. I told her I would.

I still get emails from Timothy Firth – the impersonator – reminding me to send my voluntary contribution in gratitude for the book club discussion. The person writing to me as Timothy probably knows it is not coming. I have a feeling the scammers know I am on to them because of how the meeting ended. After running through all the questions they had prepared, the moderator asked if I had any final comments.

I asked if any of them had thoughts to share about the last chapter in my book. Reported from fake call centres in Delhi, I explained, it is the story of ambitious young people being drawn into an underworld of scams and fraud.

“It is happening all over the world,” she said, “including in Africa.”
paragraphs: Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch This piece first appeared in the Dial

‘Hello Professor Snigdha Poonam,” the email began. I read that again. Nobody has ever called me “professor” for the obvious reason that I am not a professor. Bracing myself, I read on. The email was from Timothy Firth, organiser of a Seattle-based life-drawing community with 1,943 members that regularly has “thoughtful discussions inspired by creative works”. A recent inspiration was my first book, Dreamers: How Young Indians Are Changing Their World . The group wanted to discuss it, the email said, at one of its upcoming meetups. Attendees would be encouraged to post reviews on Goodreads and Amazon after.

I looked up CAM Life Drawing and found an events page and an Instagram account. The latter had some photos of Timothy Firth – white, male – as well as testimonials from members who said he worked “day and night to create more community space”. Something told me this wasn’t the man who had reached out to me.

Why would a hyperlocal life-drawing community in Seattle be interested in a nonfiction book about the shifting aspirations of young people in India’s small towns? The book was published seven years ago. What did they want from me?

I accepted the invitation. The next email had a slick poster promoting the Zoom event, with the book cover as the backdrop and blurbs from the Economist and other publications. My attention was drawn to something more intriguing: a request for a “contribution fee”, with no amount specified. It would cover promotion, coordination and administration. But, oddly, this email didn’t come from Timothy. Signing off this time was Stephen – “Organiser, Community Improv LA”, which was another group in another city. According to the improv community’s Facebook group, Stephen is indeed the name of the organiser. However, Stephen had written to me using Timothy’s email address. To add to the chaos, Stephen/Timothy had also left what I suspect was an AI prompt in the email, which included the line: “MAKE IT MORE PROFESSIONAL.”
This was undoubtedly a scam. Genuine book clubs don’t ask for money from authors. But who was behind it?

Had these individuals actually read my work, they would have wanted to stay away from me. I have spent the last 10 years reporting on transnational fraud. My first book, Dreamers, closed with a chapter on fake call centres in India; my second, Scamlands, travelled to other low-income countries in Asia to portray an invisible empire that thrives on inequality, technological change and the erosion of trust.

Along the way, I met and interviewed the scammers whose labour keeps this empire running. For some, fraud was a route to upward mobility; for others, an act of revenge against the privileged. Though I have formally emerged from this underworld, I can never delete a scam email without wanting to know more.

I agreed to pay the book club – but after rather than before the event. After clarifying that “Stephen” was a typing error, “Timothy” sent me a Google Meet link for the book discussion. I joined the meeting to find about 20 people already in there: Alexander, Andrew, Mira, Rajnish, another Alexander, and several others. Timothy was also there and so was Stephen. None of them had their cameras on. Going by the profile pictures they used, most of them appeared to be white.
“Professor, what did you learn while reporting from Indian small towns?”

While the questions may have been AI-generated, the voices seemed human. They did not always align with their pictures. Timothy seemed to be a woman, not a man, judging by the voice. Who were these people? They left only one clue. All these ostensibly white people, men and women, spoke with a west African accent.

I am not the only author to have found myself stuck in a Zoom book club with fake readers. Countless writers with published books have been receiving invitations from reading communities that start to unravel after a basic Google search.

As often happens with scams, most invitations sound too good to be true – thousands of members, incredible Goodreads clout and, at times, something even more alluring for an author: a deep understanding of their book.

One author who engaged with a book-club impersonator was told a $100 (£75) contribution for the online event would cover snacks for the participants; she withdrew without asking how they would partake of the snacks while on Zoom. Novelist Marsh Rose, playing along, exchanged 29 emails with the Chicago LGBTQ Book Club. “The individuals whose voices I heard on the Zoom didn’t seem to be speaking from Chicago. They all sounded like my friend in Nigeria,” she wrote in a blog post for WritersWeekly.com, an online resource for authors that offers writing opportunities and industry news.

Writers are also being bombarded with offers to publish our next book, market our book, handle social media for us, represent us as agents and get us book-to-movie deals with Netflix and Paramount. Every major publisher, agent, editor, author union and literary award executive is at risk of being impersonated.

The money requested often seems small. “Amounts reported to me range from $55 to $350. In one case, the scammer offered three ‘spotlight packages’ – basic, essential and premium – for between $100 and $200,” Victoria Strauss, co-founder of Writer Beware, an anti-scam watchdog, wrote in a blog post. Often, the paper trail leads to Nigerian third parties holding bank accounts in the US. Author Jon Cocks paid $478.65 to one “Mary Brown ,” who claimed a wide network of book clubs across the US, the UK and Australia, only to later notice the name Dayo Oguntuase listed as the recipient on the PayPal statement.

The Writers’ Guild of Great Britain (WGGB) reports “an explosion” in the number of members seeking advice about unusually enticing offers in recent months. “Even the most vigilant of writers are understandably falling prey to these scams,” WGGB’s general secretary, Ellie Piers, said in a statement commenting on new guidance, co-issued with the Society of Authors in May, to help authors protect themselves against scammers. “Our advisory team receives at least a dozen reports of scams each week,” Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors, said in her own statement, tracing the spike to the emergence of generative AI. The US Authors Guild says it hears from authors who have been scammed, or nearly scammed, every day. Angela Hoy, the founder of WritersWeekly.com, told me she is in touch with “authors all day long, every day, thinking they got an offer from one of the top five publishers in New York or thinking they’ve been contacted by a famous literary agent”.

The scale of the operation became clear after US authorities launched an investigation into the business. According to the Department of Justice, more than 800 authors were defrauded of upwards of $48m (£36m). Writer Beware received hundreds of complaints about PageTurner. One author reportedly lost more than $600,000 (£450,000). The prosecutors found that at least $42m in proceeds were laundered through accounts in the Philippines. One defendant pleaded guilty in May of this year, while three others are awaiting trial.

Judging by the surge in both the number and range of baits used on authors over the past couple of years, the scams seem to be launched from multiple territories. Anyone who has researched publishing would know most authors don’t have bundles of cash lying around. So why are the scammers coming after us?

Hoy, who has dealt with thousands of writers at WritersWeekly.com, puts it down to ego. Brian Whiddon, the site’s managing editor, elaborated: “Not every author is a narcissist, but they all want to be recognised. That’s exactly what these scammers are targeting. They have identified a very, very lucrative niche.”

Writers are waiting “for somebody to read their writing”, Hoy added. She argued that is why many writers believe the praise scammers heap on them. AI makes many of the compliments sound nuanced and personalised. Elderly authors are particularly vulnerable. As Hoy explained, a significant number of people who have a book in them leave off the writing until they have retired. Something else also kicks into the picture at this life stage: a sizable retirement fund. Scammers know American people have worked their whole lives and have retirement accounts, Hoy said.

Some authors are so hell-bent on signing up for the deals the scammers promise that they disregard Hoy’s counsel. Others come to Hoy when it’s too late. She has said one of the writers in her community paid more than $100,000 for a fake book-to-movie deal.
Even as a new category of literary scams emerges every few days, authors have very little information about the people behind them.

In August, Danny de Hek, a New Zealand-based scam buster, forwarded me an Excel spreadsheet he received from a scammer in Karachi, Pakistan , with permission from the sender. Titled “LinkedIn Outreach 2026”, it has monthly data on targeted authors from March until August. One sheet has 403 names, each neatly labelled: new author, cookbook author, religious author, investigative author, poetry author, New York Times bestselling author and so on. Most are based in the US; the rest are in Canada, Australia or Europe.

It’s an incredibly detailed document, with columns for the name of the person who found the profile, the person who first reached out, the service the author needs (website development, illustrator, social media visibility), the department handling the author, meeting links shared with the author. In a few cases, the document also lists the outcome of the outreach.
“Meeting booked Wed 12 Aug, 10pm PKT, number confirmed, deep trust-built relationship, ready to invest, needs custom package built around limited budget and multi-project scope.”

Some of the details only make sense if you know the context. 10pm PKT would mean 10am on the US west coast and 1pm in the east. Danny told me that most of the people working on this scam are Pakistani, yet the names of the callers are all American-sounding – Ashley, Jocelyn, Megan – probably to fool the authors into thinking they are Americans working for US-based companies and groups.

Scam recipients often find the emails they receive haphazard and random. But the modern scam industry is a highly organised system modelled on the global corporate setup, with clearly laid out deliverables, salaries, incentives and reporting structures. Even though the schemes are mind-boggling in range, the young people joining these “companies” are given the same targets: Americans on top, followed by gullible foreigners in other western countries. I spent several years reporting from India on its massive scam call-centre network, which employs hundreds of thousands of educated young people trying to beat the dim economic prospects offered by the domestic labour market. Similar Excel spreadsheets are used to organise schemes where Indian scammers in Delhi or Kolkata impersonate Microsoft tech support, the Internal Revenue Service or even the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

De Hek, who exposes transnational scams on his blog and YouTube channel with relentless zeal, told me Pakistan’s fake companies offering literary services operate in a similar fashion to India’s scam call centres. The majority of them maintain physical offices in Karachi and Lahore and employ people aged 20 to 24. Upon joining, the young employees typically get assigned to a unit, each designed around a specific literary swindle. While entry-level employees may only be tasked with outreach, the more experienced ones are entrusted with building long-term relationships aimed at selling multiple “packages” to clients over months and sometimes years.

The most profitable service targets authors lurking outside the notoriously gatekept realm of traditional publishing. Rather than through a cold call or email, the scammers lure them through websites offering self-publishing or vanity publishing.

Scam companies in Pakistan trap writers by impersonating known publishing houses and paying thousands of dollars to influence search results on Google. As a result, someone with a finished manuscript who searches online may find sites such as penguinwriters.com or amazonglobalpublishers.com before any legitimate self-publishing platform. Unlike traditional publishing websites, these feature open calls for new writers. WritersWeekly.com estimates there are at least 3,000 such sites. The biggest tell: a chat box pops up in the bottom right of all fake publishing websites as soon as the page opens, followed by a message from someone with an American-sounding name (such as Mark Anderson or Jessica Parker) and a white person’s face: “How can I help you today?” “Talk to a live agent, not a bot!” claims a ticker. And that much is absolutely true: the person messaging you is a scammer whose shift is dictated by the waking hours in your time zone.

None of the five major trade publishers has sued alleged impersonators. The only recorded instance involves Amazon, which took nearly 20 individuals and associated companies to court in California for falsely claiming affiliation with Amazon Publishing and Kindle Direct Publishing to deceive authors. Amazon won $36.4m (£27m) in February 2025.

M L Stark, a Danish self-published author of several psychological thrillers, is one of the rare victims who has met – and confronted – her scammer in person. Last year, she flew to Thailand to meet with Ethan Williams, a man she believed had become her longtime editor at an LA-based self-publishing house affiliated with Amazon – and a close friend. By this time, she had been talking to him over Zoom and email for more than a year and paid his company about $100,000 for different author services, from editing and cover design to coverage in the New York Times and the Los Angeles Times .

While most of the services she paid for never materialised, the company did follow through on some. They signed her up on IngramSpark, a self-publishing platform, which enabled her to release two books, and Amazon, which made the books available on the platform. Most notably, in 2024, one of her titles was displayed on a digital billboard in Times Square.

“I had paid $10,000 for that,” she told me. Only later, she told me, did she come to see these deliveries as strategic concessions, held back for moments when a long-term client reached the end of her tether. “Each time, it happened when I told them, after months of them stalling, that I wanted my money back.”

The scammers’ last pitch was a Netflix adaptation that they claimed the film-makers wanted to shoot in Thailand – an important setting in her upcoming book, a thriller based on her own life. Stark and Williams were meeting in Thailand to scout locations.

He had told her he was a British citizen, half English and half Arab; as a light-skinned Pakistani, his story was plausible. “He is an artist, he knew how to play the role,” she said. Still, she asked him to show an ID. He produced one that looked clearly faked. “I demanded he show me his passport,” she said. That exposed his real name and citizenship. He came clean. “He said, ‘Yeah, this has been a scam from the beginning. Even Peter is using a fake name; even Ronald is using a fake name. Everybody in the company that you have talked to is a scammer. It’s a huge scam operation, and we are not based in Los Angeles. We are based in Karachi.’” She is still processing her shock.

I clicked on a random website from a list of known scam sites; it happened to be impersonating Red Rock, a real literary agency based in London whose authors have been published by major publishers such as Hurst, which published my first book in the UK. Bold promises greeted me on the homepage.

A chat window opened, and someone with the username “Rae Donnaelly” asked how she could help. I told her I had an idea for a book. She asked for my contact, then called me on WhatsApp from a US number. She spoke like a South Asian imitating an American accent, something I could easily recognise because I’m South Asian myself, and we’ve all tried it at one point or another.
I told her the truth: I was writing an article about author-baiting scams, and I was hoping she could tell me about her experience working for a fake publishing house.
She told me she wasn’t “authorised” to talk about the company she works for, and she refused to tell me her real name. But she had no qualms spilling the beans on her ex-employer.

Rae has a law degree but found it difficult to find a job in law after university. Her first job after graduating was at a fake publishing company in Karachi. “I started working for a company which was a scam – a guaranteed scam – and I didn’t know it when I started off with them. I was an intern trying to learn how the system really works; what the pros and cons are.”

It took Rae only a few days to figure out the company’s business model: proxy sales. They would tell the author they would get them a guaranteed sale order for 1,000 copies, or something like that, making “fake commitments”. The scam rarely stopped there. After a client signed up for developmental editing, they would be offered a discount on book-cover design, and once they paid for that, the scammer would dangle social media management. “It could start off from as little as $400- $500, and it could go up to the skies, like $10,000, $15,000.”

As with all scams, those executing the con learned how easily people can be manipulated if you know what they desired. “You could see how the human brain works. It’s actually scary when you think about it,” Rae admitted.
She believes Americans make easy scam targets. “People in the US are very nice, they’re very good-hearted people. They trust you. Whatever you’re saying, they trust you. That’s the problem.”

At times, the clients only noticed they had been scammed after they had paid all the way up to a Times Square display and Broadway adaptation. “When the authors did not see results, they would either reverse the charge on their card or accuse us of being scamsters,” Rae recalled.

According to Talal Choudhary, an Islamabad-based tech journalist, there are about 1,000 Pakistani companies running scam sites. “One company runs as many as 25 websites. I personally know a company that had about 200 employees, just offering services to writers.” These companies are “very, very profitable”, he said. “From one client, you can make $60,000.”

So that’s what they did. They just ripped people off.”

Convinced he was part of the suspected author-scam network, she made him an offer of her own: write an article for Writersweekly.com about how the company he worked for scams Americans while being based overseas.

But he wrote it using AI, which is against the site’s submission rules. He also ignored the brief. Instead, he chose to highlight, as Hoy recalls, “how it’s so hard for people in Africa and therefore it’s OK to scam Americans because all of us are rich over here”.

articles.content:
Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’

A round lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.

Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.

The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.

It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.

Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.

Asked by a reporter whether he had a response to Obama, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House”, Trump spent nearly two full minutes explaining that the work had been done by the “finest artisans”, that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” – a racist trope – and that Trump himself only spends “five minutes a day, 10 minutes a day” addressing the problem. ( Later that day , he spent another 10 minutes talking about it.)

But the framing of the question – posed by a reporter for LindellTV, founded by the Trump-supporting My Pillow founder Mike Lindell – pointed to what has become a rightwing talking point: the out-of-touch Obama, these critics claim, was mocking restaurant for regular people. The Cheesecake Factory isn’t cheap – a burger will run you about $20 – but it’s positioned as a treat that won’t break the bank.

The conservative political strategist Corinne Clark Barron tweeted : “KEEP THE CHEESECAKE FACTORY OUT OF YOUR ELITIST MOUTH.” On CNN , the New York Post columnist Lydia Moynihan said the remarks showed “how elitist he and the party that he continues to lead has become”. On Fox News, a chyron announced : “Obama criticized for Cheesecake Factory ‘snobbery’.”

This seems to deliberately misconstrue the joke’s primary target, which was the president, not the restaurant. It also conveniently forgets the first half, about Saddam Hussein, who was not known for minimalist taste. Nevertheless, the pitchforks were out, and the Trump administration deployed a true man of the people – the treasury secretary and hedge fund founder Scott Bessent – to dine there.

In fact, he “always” does, as he was at great pains to point out . “I had a great meal, always have a great meal,” he told a Fox Business reporter. He ordered “what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger”. Bessent, whose net worth is roughly $600m , said he would “tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try”.

The median home price in Beverly Hills, home to the first Cheesecake Factory, is $4m; the restaurant itself is far more affordable than the 90210 zip code might suggest. But as Bessent himself proved, the restaurant’s clientele includes plenty of elites: Jennifer Lawrence, Miley Cyrus and Drake are all reportedly fans. It’s a stretch to suggest Obama was punching down here.

That said, given the fierce devotion the restaurant inspires, Obama was perhaps taking a risk even mentioning it – especially at a time when the cost of living is on the ballot. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that soundbite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” Rick McCormack, who helped create the restaurant’s decor, told CNN’s David Mack. Odes to the restaurant and its “affordable opulence”, as Mack puts it, abound.

In the Atlantic , Elaine Godfrey praises its “sumptuousness: the orange, inviting glow from the knobbly chandeliers; the floral frescoes and painted columns; the generous fountain pops and the dense wedges of cake”. A Redditor puts it more simply: “I can eat the whole plate of food like a savage and waddle to my car afterward with a piece of cheesecake to go.” The food is indeed good, and plentiful: the chain is known for its enormous and diverse menu, with items ranging from fried mac and cheese to avocado egg rolls to vegan cobb salad. There’s also, of course, lots of cheesecake, including but not limited to the mind-boggling Oreo Dream Extreme. On Tuesday, the chain reported third-quarter revenue of $1.03bn, up from $907.2m a year before. It’s routinely named among Fortune’s 100 best companies to work for.

In short, everyone loves the Cheesecake Factory, from Birmingham, Alabama, to Des Moines, Iowa, to Beverly Hills, where the autumn sun shone this week over warm baskets of complimentary bread. Surely it can take a joke.
paragraphs: Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’

A round lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.
Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.
The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.

It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.

Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.

Asked by a reporter whether he had a response to Obama, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House”, Trump spent nearly two full minutes explaining that the work had been done by the “finest artisans”, that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” – a racist trope – and that Trump himself only spends “five minutes a day, 10 minutes a day” addressing the problem. ( Later that day , he spent another 10 minutes talking about it.)

But the framing of the question – posed by a reporter for LindellTV, founded by the Trump-supporting My Pillow founder Mike Lindell – pointed to what has become a rightwing talking point: the out-of-touch Obama, these critics claim, was mocking restaurant for regular people. The Cheesecake Factory isn’t cheap – a burger will run you about $20 – but it’s positioned as a treat that won’t break the bank.

The conservative political strategist Corinne Clark Barron tweeted : “KEEP THE CHEESECAKE FACTORY OUT OF YOUR ELITIST MOUTH.” On CNN , the New York Post columnist Lydia Moynihan said the remarks showed “how elitist he and the party that he continues to lead has become”. On Fox News, a chyron announced : “Obama criticized for Cheesecake Factory ‘snobbery’.”

This seems to deliberately misconstrue the joke’s primary target, which was the president, not the restaurant. It also conveniently forgets the first half, about Saddam Hussein, who was not known for minimalist taste. Nevertheless, the pitchforks were out, and the Trump administration deployed a true man of the people – the treasury secretary and hedge fund founder Scott Bessent – to dine there.

In fact, he “always” does, as he was at great pains to point out . “I had a great meal, always have a great meal,” he told a Fox Business reporter. He ordered “what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger”. Bessent, whose net worth is roughly $600m , said he would “tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try”.

The median home price in Beverly Hills, home to the first Cheesecake Factory, is $4m; the restaurant itself is far more affordable than the 90210 zip code might suggest. But as Bessent himself proved, the restaurant’s clientele includes plenty of elites: Jennifer Lawrence, Miley Cyrus and Drake are all reportedly fans. It’s a stretch to suggest Obama was punching down here.

That said, given the fierce devotion the restaurant inspires, Obama was perhaps taking a risk even mentioning it – especially at a time when the cost of living is on the ballot. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that soundbite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” Rick McCormack, who helped create the restaurant’s decor, told CNN’s David Mack. Odes to the restaurant and its “affordable opulence”, as Mack puts it, abound.

In the Atlantic , Elaine Godfrey praises its “sumptuousness: the orange, inviting glow from the knobbly chandeliers; the floral frescoes and painted columns; the generous fountain pops and the dense wedges of cake”. A Redditor puts it more simply: “I can eat the whole plate of food like a savage and waddle to my car afterward with a piece of cheesecake to go.” The food is indeed good, and plentiful: the chain is known for its enormous and diverse menu, with items ranging from fried mac and cheese to avocado egg rolls to vegan cobb salad. There’s also, of course, lots of cheesecake, including but not limited to the mind-boggling Oreo Dream Extreme. On Tuesday, the chain reported third-quarter revenue of $1.03bn, up from $907.2m a year before. It’s routinely named among Fortune’s 100 best companies to work for.

In short, everyone loves the Cheesecake Factory, from Birmingham, Alabama, to Des Moines, Iowa, to Beverly Hills, where the autumn sun shone this week over warm baskets of complimentary bread. Surely it can take a joke.

articles.title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence

The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’

An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.

The 66-year-old, who won the Palme d’Or at Cannes last year for It Was Just an Accident , was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.

The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned to Iran in March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.

A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.

Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.

Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.

Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year, Panahi warned that the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.

“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”

The latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.

The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated film The Seed of the Sacred Fig , told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”

Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.

She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.

The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”

In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.

articles.title: Vegetarian coconut curry recipes: Maunika Gowardhan’s spicy aubergine baingan and spiced vegetable stew
articles.summary: Aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves, and a gingery vegetable stew with coconut and green chillies Both these hearty curries use coconut as part of their base gravy. The region of Kutch in Gujarat is brimming with vegetable curries, and the bhagare baingan features many classic Kutchi ingredients; it has several similarities to the Hyderabadi version, too. Avial , meanwhile, is often served at celebrations in south India, and this version is a Keralan recipe made with a flavourful coconut paste. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves, and a gingery vegetable stew with coconut and green chillies

B oth these hearty curries use coconut as part of their base gravy. The region of Kutch in Gujarat is brimming with vegetable curries, and the bhagare baingan features many classic Kutchi ingredients; it has several similarities to the Hyderabadi version, too. I’ve used baby aubergines, but if need be you can use regular diced aubergines instead. Avial , meanwhile, is often served at celebrations in south India, and this version is a Keralan recipe made with a flavourful coconut paste.

For the paste 1 tbsp poppy seeds 2 tbsp vegetable oil 90g finely chopped white onion 1 tbsp sesame seeds 1 tbsp grated fresh coconut

For the gravy 160g fresh tomatoes 4 tbsp vegetable oil 150g thinly sliced white onions 5 garlic cloves , peeled and ground to a paste ¼ tsp turmeric powder 1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder 2 tsp ground cumin Salt , to taste 8-10 baby aubergines , slit open lengthways 1½ tsp tamarind paste ½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper 2 mild dried red chillies 12 fresh curry leaves Coriander , to garnish Rice or roti , to serve

For the paste, soak the poppy seeds in 70ml warm water 20 minutes. Meanwhile, put the oil in a small frying pan on a medium heat, then fry the onions for eight or nine minutes, just until they start to change colour. Add the sesame seeds and grated fresh coconut, and fry, stirring, for two minutes. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature. Once cooled, stir in the poppy seeds and their soaking liquid, then blitz the lot to a smooth paste.

Meanwhile, put the tomatoes in a blender and blitz to a smooth puree. In a large, heavy-based frying pan for which you have a lid, heat the oil over a medium heat, then add the onions and fry, stirring regularly, for 17-18 minutes, until softened and lightly browned. Add the garlic paste, fry for 20 seconds, then stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and cumin, and fry, stirring for a few seconds, until fragrant.

Add the pureed tomatoes and fry, stirring, for five minutes, until the mix splits and the oil leaves the side of the pan. Add the ground poppy seed and onion paste and fry, stirring continuously, for four minutes. Pour in 350ml warm water, season with salt to taste, then stir in the aubergines, cover and simmer on a low heat for about 15 minutes, stirring once halfway through. Add the tamarind paste and simmer for a further five minutes.

Take off the heat and stir in the black pepper, whole dried red chillies and curry leaves. Garnish with coriander and serve warm with roti or rice.

For the paste 200g grated fresh coconut 2½cm x 2½cm piece ginger , peeled and roughly chopped ½ tsp cumin seeds 1 green bird’s eye chilli

For the curry 3 tbsp vegetable oil 1 tsp black mustard seeds 1 dried mild chilli , roughly broken into pieces 7-8 fresh curry leaves 70g finely chopped white onion 1 tsp turmeric powder 200g medium carrots , peeled and cut into 1cm dice 150g potato (use a good all-rounder such as red rooster), peeled and cut into 1cm dice 200g french beans , all topped and cut into three roughly equal pieces ½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper Salt , to taste 3 tbsp greek yoghurt Coriander , to garnish Rice or paratha , to serve

For the paste, put the fresh coconut, ginger, cumin seeds and chilli in a blender, add 200ml water and blitz to a smooth paste.

Put the oil in a heavy-based saucepan on a medium heat. Add the mustard seeds, dried chilli and curry leaves. After 15 or so seconds, when they start to splutter and pop, add the chopped onions and fry, stirring, for seven or eight minutes, until they start to soften. Add the turmeric and the chopped carrots and potatoes, fry, stirring, for just a few seconds, then pour in 200ml water, cover and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook gently for 10 minutes, then add the chopped green beans and cook for another eight minutes, until all the vegetables are tender.

Add the coconut paste and the ground black pepper, season with salt to taste, then stir and simmer for another two minutes. Whisk the yoghurt, then stir it into the pan and simmer for a minute more. Garnish with coriander and serve at once with rice or paratha.

Maunika Gowardhan’s most recent book, Curry: Recipes from Indian Home Kitchens, is published by Quadrille at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, go to guardianbookshop.com
